You might be thinking, if you're the optimistic sort, that today's official unveiling of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel means that wheels are turning and things are happening and you're going to be off to Hammerfell soon—or at the very least, learning more about what's coming in Bethesda's next big RPG. Alas, in a follow-up post on social media, the studio made it clear that you shouldn't start holding your breath just yet.

"Thank you for 40 years of shared memories," Bethesda wrote. "We can't wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it'll be some time before we're ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you."

Thank you for 40 years of shared memories. We can’t wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it’ll be some time before we’re ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you.

"Some time" is obviously not a defined span, but I find that generally speaking it's a nicer, more politic way of saying "long time"—for instance, you could say it's been "some time" since Bethesda first announced the Elder Scrolls 6, and yeah, that's true. It was also eight freakin' years ago, and we've heard basically nothing since.

That is, very roughly, the same amount of time Bethesda needed to make the first Elder Scrolls game, Arena, as well as Daggerfall, Morrowind, the Morrowind expansions Tribunal and Bloodmoon, and the spinoff games Battlespire and Redguard. If you're (relatively) new to the series, eight years represents the span between Oblivion and The Elder Scrolls Online, a stretch interspersed by Skyrim and five major expansions: Knights of the Nine and Shivering Isles for Oblivion, and Dawnguard, Hearthfire, and Dragonborn for Skyrim.

Of course, Bethesda's had other things on the go over the past eight years too. Todd Howard said shortly after The Elder Scrolls 6 reveal that it was in pre-production, while Starfield was in full production. Starfield was Bethesda's top priority in the years leading up to its 2023 release; Howard later said that they'd just wanted to answer the fan question (are you making a new Elder Scrolls?) that came up every time they announced something else, like Starfield.

"Just pretend we didn't announce it," he joked. "Doesn't exist. No one's heard a word."How long Sentinel will take to get from here to launch is anybody's guess, although Bloomberg's Jason Schreier said on Bluesky that it's "still more than two years away." When questioned about his prediction, Schreier asserted that it's not a prediction at all, and that he knows "the time frame the game is targeting."

#3779. Arkane devs say Microsoft is ‘sabotaging’ Marvel’s Blade as the studio is ‘profitable, just not profitable enough’

Development on Marvel’s Blade at Arkane Lyon is “going fine,” but the studio is still at risk of closure “because, and only because, Microsoft decided to, even if that means sabotaging the game it funded,” according to a new statement.

This comes today from Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo, a union of workers at Arkane, in a pretty scathing statement about the publisher’s ongoing attempts to sell the studio as part of its “reset” throughout the year, or close it entirely.

“Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons,” the statement continued. “But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist. Because after freezing hiring for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost, Microsoft now uses those same delay and additional cost as a reason to close down the studio.”

Yesterday, Bloomberg reported that Ubisoft and two other companies are in the bidding for Arkane, which has found success in the past with franchises like Dishonored and Prey. Marvel’s Blade was revealed nearly three years ago but hasn’t been heard from since.

“The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals,” the statement said. “In the wake of thousands of yearly firings, studio closure to which you can now add the tenth of thousands of voluntary buyout offered by the company, the decision to close Arkane is solely the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization. Arkane is profitable. Just not profitable enough for Microsoft.”

The prevailing thought is that if Microsoft doesn’t find a suitable offer for Arkane, the studio will close down, and Blade may end up canceled in a similar situation to EA closing down BioWare and ending development on Mass Effect Universe last month.

#3778. Dune: Awakening's free Blood and Ice expansion swaps sand for snow on 1st December

Funcom's survival MMO Dune: Awakening is heading north with a free expansion that trades the deserts of Arrakis for a frozen new map.

The expansion, called Blood and Ice, will release on 1st December. Funcom said it adds "around 35 hours of new progression", along with new vehicle modules, augments, and specialisation traits. It's coming to PC, PS5, and Xbox.

The new map, called the Polar Sink, turns the game's usual survival loop upside down. Instead of protecting yourself from extreme heat, you'll need to find ways to stay warm, upgrading your gear with resources found only in the Polar Sink.

The map is split into two biomes, the tundra and the ice cap. You'll start in the tundra, where wealthy water shipper families have built lavish strongholds, before trying to get into the heavily guarded ice cap. Once you're in, you can harvest ice to cool your base equipment and speed up production.

According to Funcom, the expansion "brings the focus back to ground-level survival, with traversal, temperature management, and combat all playing important roles in your progression". The studio also said future updates will add more reasons to go back to the region.

Blood and Ice also brings a new Events tab to the main menu. Shortly after the expansion launches, a new event called Water Crisis will follow the current one, The Scourge. Funcom says every event can be completed in both single-player and multiplayer, and that it plans to run them more often, each with new stories and free rewards.

Funcom has also launched a cosmetics store, which it says will help fund continued development and free updates. The store will start with a rotating selection of items, including looks taken from the Dune films to coincide with Dune: Part Three's release in cinemas this December. The plan is to eventually make the full catalogue available at all times.

Several of the community's most-requested features are also on the way. Offline single-player is due this month, and from January 2027 you'll be able to copy characters from multiplayer servers to single-player, and from single-player to select private or self-hosted servers on PC. Full cross-play will also arrive in January 2027.

"We're far from done," Funcom said, adding that it has "ambitious plans for the year ahead", including major free updates in 2027. The studio says more than a million new players have joined since the game launched on consoles, alongside a rebuilt endgame, three DLCs, and the conclusion of the game's first story arc, Book One.

Just a couple of weeks ago, Norwegian developer Funcom, creator of Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles - and many other games - confirmed it was entering a period of restructuring and bracing for layoffs as a result. You may remember the company making a similar move this time last year, months after the initial PC release of Dune: Awakening.

Bethesda has finally given us the tiniest morsels of information about The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, including the title and a few teasers about the lore. #3776. The Dark Souls Devs Are Masters At Looney Tunes–Style Physical Comedy

I used to think that Dark Souls was a very serious game. A serious, serious game for serious, hardcore gamers. Grimdark, full of esoteric mysteries and depressing, philosophical themes. Tragedy in every sense. No hope for its characters. Any shred of light snuffed out by the encroaching shadow.

I have been delighted to learn in more recent years that this is actually wrong, and Dark Souls (and its sequels, both real and spiritual) are actually comedy games. Dark Souls is video-game Looney Tunes.

— Rebekah Valentine (@duckvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-10-30T04:27:18.287Z

What the fuck is that?! A skeleton attached to a wheel of bones? A bonewheel? I guess?!

Yeah, that’s some of the funniest shit I’ve ever seen. It’s basically just this:

A lot of games try really hard to be funny via attempts at witty writing or quippy characters. Some succeed, some fail. But with Dark Souls (and Elden Ring, which I played a few years ago), FromSoftware proves it is is superb at something I imagine must be incredibly difficult to do in video games: physical comedy. You have to take into account player movement, enemy AI, objects getting caught on one anotherâthe delicate dance required to make a physical gag happen in a game like this takes such an expert hand. And yet, FromSoftware manages to Wile E. Coyote the player into incredible slapstick moments over and over, through clever use of environmental hazards and very smart enemy placement within them. You can’t tell me that reaching a tight corner and looking carefully around it just to see this sort of bullshit isn’t funny:

— Rebekah Valentine (@duckvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-11-01T03:17:26.196Z

Yes, many (most) of these scenarios result in player death, which can be frustrating, but how can I be mad at dying if my death was absolutely hilarious? How can anyone at all be mad when your death animation looks this stupid?

— Rebekah Valentine (@duckvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-09-10T01:47:56.059Z

It’s even better when it’s self-inflicted, which it so often is. Dark Souls is full of such clunky, clumsy movement that often, one wrong step will send you into the abyss, and it will be all your fault. Two nights ago, I lost over 30,000 souls because I accidentally dodge-rolled off an easy-to-traverse cliff on a corpse run. Sometimes, you just jump off ledges for no reason beyond your own incompetence:

— Rebekah Valentine (@duckvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-09-09T03:28:58.157Z

And I do think the comedy works all the betterÂ because Dark Souls is such a tragic story. Most of the good NPCs die ignobly, the evil ones either die after a hell of a struggle or become even worse, then die, and no one ever accomplishes their goals without a terrible cost or a monkey’s paw curling. ItÂ is the grimdark depression adventure that was billed to me, it’s justÂ also a sketch from early ’90s Sunday morning kids’ TV at the same time. It’s funny to fall off a cliff, it’s even funnier if you fall off because you got jump-scared by a freakin’ wheel made of a skeleton.

Whoever at FromSoftware is responsible for skeleton placement, I would love to interview you on this subject. Please contact me. Just whoever is the person who decides where skeletons go.

Three cheers, then, for the regular skeleton and the giant skeleton, the giant mosquitos, the mushroom people, those goddamn basilisks (may they rot in hell), the many zombie guys, and whatever that weird blob of dudes with spears surrounding that one statue in the painted world was. I love you all. And especially, most especially, three cheers for Bonewheels. I’m still not done with Dark Souls, and I hope I haven’t seen the last of you.

#3775. Footage of a Persona 1 remake has seemingly leaked online

Almost two minutes of footage from what appears to be a remake of the original Persona has leaked online.

The clip, which seemingly gives the remake the subtitle Be Your True Mind, was shared on the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit. It was uploaded to file-sharing site Gofile on 31st October under a Japanese filename that translates as "Megami Ibunroku Persona Remake".

Interestingly, the footage looks a lot like Atlus' more recent entries. It shows off stylish menus and a brief look at combat that closely resembles Persona 5 and Persona 3 Reload. There's also a short social link cutscene in a noticeably different, almost graphic novel art style.

Fans digging through the clip believe they have spotted several details that lend it credibility. These include what looks like Unreal Engine debug text in the top left corner during battle (Atlus switched to Unreal Engine for Persona 3 Reload), a new remix of the original PlayStation game's Pandora theme, and the protagonist being referred to as "Boy With Earring", which is how he is named in Persona 2: Eternal Punishment.

Atlus has not announced a Persona 1 remake, and we can't verify the footage, so treat all of this with the usual caveats.

How do you solve a problem like Persona 4? At Gamescom, we sat down with series director Kazuhisa Wada to talk about the Persona 4 Remake, and ask about how Atlus is approaching the original text for the remake.

Welcome to FOV 90, an FPS column from staff writer Morgan Park. Every other week, I cover topics relevant to first-person shooter enjoyers, spanning everything from multiplayer and singleplayer to the old and the new.

Welcome back to a special election day edition of FOV 90, the only FPS column that insists American readers vote twice today—first on important videogame matters right here, then on crucial *gestures at everything else* matters at your designated polling place.

Today we return from a totally planned hiatus, during which the PC Gamer community settled both the best RTS unit and best horror games, to dispute an issue of far greater significance: The greatest FPS mode of all time. Round 2's matchups reflected an enthusiasm for classic team-based formats with a respectable turnout as well for modern arrivals like Battle Royale. I asked you to make some tough calls and you showed up.

Over 2,500 votes were cast across Round 2 matchups, and the results are in.

A decisive victory in each contest. Every mode I voted for came out on top, which I honestly didn't expect. Sure, TDM over Battle Royale makes sense, but an 82% majority tells me that the most popular shooter format of today has not usurped the classics among PC Gamer readers (same). But even so, this is where I expected Conquest (a chaotic fight over territory) to accept a humble defeat to Bomb Defusal (the gold standard of competitive PvP). I'm glad I was wrong!

Not as much comment sparring went down this time, but I would like to highlight one reader comment that got me thinking:

And here's how PC Gamer's staff reacted to the results:

"What's notable to me about the final four is that they mostly don't put individuals on the spot. In Infection, Battle Royale, and Bomb Defusal, you can wind up being the last survivor, with all the pressure on you to bring it home. That's not really the case in TDM, Conquest, Payload, or CTF, which usually allow unlimited respawns (or in the case of Conquest, end when respawns run out). CTF does require individual flag runner heroism, but as part of a team effort."

"The continued dominance of Payload is vexing to me: I've always thought it was Fine, but an all-conquering hero? Maybe I'm just sore it bodied Gun Game in the first round—I was a fan back when it was a modded Counter-Strike mode first and foremost. If Payload beats out the all time classic, Capture the Flag, this round, we may have to reexamine this whole "democracy" thing."

"CTF had its time, and was at its peak in the various iterations of Tribes, a context in which you could literally swoop in to snatch the banner. But I don't think it stands up if we're evaluating these as modern modes. Otherwise, it's tough to see Bomb Defusal fizzle—Counter-Strike's competitive mode holds up wonderfully as the premier FPS esport, which says a lot given that it's asymmetrical."

But alas, it's time to bury our dead and move on. Round 3 is on!

Read up on the matchups below and vote for your favorite. Round 3 voting closes on Sunday, November 8 at 11:59 PM PDT. The more votes we get, the more interesting the results, so tell your friends! Next week we'll be back to share the results and begin the FINALS.

AKA: Team Slayer (Halo) // Warfare (Hell Let Loose)

Intimate team-based action, or large-scale territory control?

AKA: It's always Payload and CTF, because they're perfect names

Two modes about escorting an object where the other team doesn't want it to go, but only one moves on.

#3772. One Of The Greatest Adventure Games Ever Is 30 Today, And It Wasn’t Made By LucasArts

During the heyday of the point-and-click adventure, there were two big names: LucasArts and Sierra. Of course Westwood and Revolution got a good few in there too, but there’s another name that all too often gets left out: Burst Studios. That’s the team behind Toonstruck, and, er, no, that was the only adventure it ever made. But damn, the Christopher Lloyd-starring mix of cartoon and FMV was a classic, and today marks the 30th anniversary of its release.

Unambiguously inspired byÂ Who Framed Roger Rabbit, which of course also starredÂ Back to the Future‘s Christopher Lloyd,Â Toonstruck was a glorious mix of hand-drawn cartoon animation and live-action video, somewhat less-than-seamlessly combined in what still felt like a technical marvel in 1996.

It’s all very meta at the start. Lloyd plays Drew Blanc (sorry), a cartoonist who is condemned to work on the saccharine Fluffy Fluffy Bun Bun Show, and is slowly losing his mind. His boss, played by Ben Stein (sorry about that, too), drags him back into work one night and demands that he create a collection of new bunnies for the show before the morning, but Lloyd can’t stop thinking about the character he wished he were working on, purple thing Flux Wildly. Then, er, he’s sucked into his TV and finds himself trapped in a cartoon city called Cutopia. Flux is there (and voiced by none other than Dan Castellaneta!), there’s an evil Count Nefarious in the nearby area of the Malevolands, and between the two lies Flux’s homeland, lunatic town Zanydu. Nefarious, voiced by the wondrous Tim Curry, is turning all cute things evil, and it’s up to Blanc and Flux to save the day.

Yes, the premise is stone-cold insane. And perfectly so. Toonstruck is a celebration of the anarchic nature of early-20th-century cartoons, and it takes the silly subject incredibly seriously. Along with the astonishing cast already mentioned, it also featured some of the best voice actors in the industry in smaller rolesâthe likes of David Ogden Stiers (MASH), Dom DeLuise (The Cannonball Run,Â An American Tail) and Jeff Bennett (Johnny Bravo himself). And their quality is paired with the animation, celebrating everything from Tex Avery to Disney with both love and irreverence.

Even the puzzles are great! Well, apart from a couple. But it was a mid-’90s adventure game, so, y’know. Also rather of its time is an incredibly uncomfortable moment in which Flux shouts out the r-slur, and there’s a peculiarly incongruent S&M scene with barnyard animals that perhaps wouldn’t make the cut today.

Infamously, there was supposed to be a sequel toÂ Toonstruck, but the original game’s development had been a deeply fraught time, and it was (undeservedly) a complete bomb on release.

Fortunately, it’s far easier to play today than it has been at most points in the previous 30 years. Previously relegated to an awkward fit in Dosbox and refusing anything after Windows XP, the game now boots beautifully via ScummVM, which is all done for you when you buy the game via Steam. It’s outrageously expensive at $20 for a three-decade-old game, but given it’s a whopping 10 hours long (huge compared to so many adventures of the time), you’ll get your money’s worth. There’s nothing else quite like it, and it deserves to be heralded alongside Day of the Tentacle andÂ Space Quest IV. Happy birthday, old friend.

#3771. Best WoW Forever add-ons to avoid AI slop

Hey @grok, build me a World of Warcraft AI add-on. But seriously, don't.

World of Warcraft: Forever marks our return to Azeroth in the good ol’ days, and nothing says “good ol’ days” better than hopping into CurseForge to look for this month’s best add-ons. Except nowadays, World of Warcraft: Forever AI add-ons are just as common as regular ones.

And there’s usually no telling who made what. Was it a developer with an AI assistant? Maybe it’s someone and their grandma. More importantly, was it created with the same attention to detail OG devs put into their add-ons?

If it seems hastily made and just the 100th copy of something else that exists, chances are you’re dealing with AI slop. So let’s choose the best handcrafted add-ons for our new journey.

Of course, not all add-ons made with (or with the help of) AI are automatically AI slop. After all, AI tools are slowly becoming a part of professional workflows in industries like coding, with human-in-the-loop ensuring shipped products function as intended.

But this is exactly where the risk of using AI add-ons lies. Just because today’s hip model (that hasn’t gone rogue) made a “working” add-on doesn’t mean it’s 100% production-ready. At the end of the day, it’s up to each person with AI add-ons. But remember:

Players have been making WoW add-ons since 2004 (others claim since the Beta of Vanilla, so serious deja vu vibes). And many devs have been in the game for years, so they know add-ons in and out. It’s no surprise some of them already made add-ons we could use with WoW: Forever if we’re a bit nervous about AI ones:

Anyone who’s ever handled an alt knows that the go-to speed-leveling strategy is to grab as many quests as you can in an area and turn them in all at once for that sweet XP rush. But while the map already reveals where the general area of a quest is located, there’s really no in-game tool that lets you know which quests are still available in that area. That’s where Questie comes in.

This add-on enhances the map so that hovering over a zone will give you an overview of the quests you completed (and, most importantly, those that are available) in that region. There’s even a “Questie’s Journey” window that shows you a list of quests by zone and even an advanced search option.

Being a reimagined take on WoW‘s original 2004 release, it’s no surprise WoW: Forever also kept its traditional UI as part of the core experience. While Blizzard did a lot of work modernizing the UI, there’s a lot to be desired in the visuals department.

And if you’re looking for a more pleasant UI to fit the game’s updated graphics, Dialogue UI is the way to go. It adds a touch more dynamism to dialogue options, with unique looks for NPC dialogue and readables on paper and metal. You can adjust camera motion for immersion, adjust font size, copy dialogue, and even display the lore of items you pick up.

If we’re in a grinding mood, sometimes it’s a hassle to click anything other than a target on the screen. And even then, you probably set a keybind to attack a particular target. So sometimes just clicking an NPC and dialogue separately can be a hassle.

This is what DialogKey – Numy Edition wants to get us away from. Basically, it lets us bind NPC interactions to keyboard buttons. Maybe you want a one-button-fits-all option for interactions, or press a number to select a dialogue option.

The grind from Level 1 to 60 will be tougher in WoW: Forever, especially now that Blizzard wants to focus more on horizontal progression. So instead of an ever-increasing level count, we’re expecting to get side content, endgame dungeons, and other opportunities to maximize our builds.

And if you’re too busy on the grind to manually check whether it’s time to train your spells or not, then What’s Training? can make that much easier for you. It enhances the UI to let you know which spells you can upgrade now, soon-ish, and far ahead, including which levels you’d have to watch out for.

WoW has been around for more than 20 years, so naturally there are just some tiny things we wish could’ve been better. But there’s just so much Blizzard could offer in terms of settings before they become a whole host of minute details we can adjust.

On the off-chance that tinkering with hundreds of options is not a problem with you, then Enhance QoL is the add-on to get. Simply put, the add-on provides more minute adjustment options to the game’s quality-of-life features, with options for character inspection, inventory management, combat, mini-map and navigation, and more.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Not to mention, the release of WoW: Forever also comes with built-in features that we usually had to use add-ons to get. These include:

While it’s true that not all AI add-ons are slop, the disturbing number of them that are makes players uninclined to use them. Anyone can use AI to make a WoW: Forever add-on, and there’s even one that lets you make add-ons while playing the game.

Players in the “r/WoWForever” subreddit already expressed concerns about low-effort AI-coded slop add-ons throughout the beta.

You can go to the WoW: Forever page at CurseForge, sort by creation date, and you’ll see new projects pop out every few refreshes. Some honest creators include AI disclosures in the descriptions, but many don’t. Others also called out a subreddit posting trend where a user would preface “I made this add-on…” as a sign an add-on was created by AI.

“For me, it isn’t that AI made it. It’s that this person and 15 others have made slightly different variations of the exact same addon,” u/blukraken wrote in one of the posts. “How many of y’all are actually testing your addons, having another AI try to break them, looking through existing GitHub repos, or researching what other developers are doing? What would make me trust that you’d even continue iterating and fixing bugs that were found?”

In a 404 Media report, Sildri Silentcrest (Warcraft Logs CEO) told Joseph Cox that Warcraft Logs is introducing a paid commercial key, as their team noticed more users scraping their data and using their API for their own projects without credit and/or proper commercial licensing.

It doesn’t help that we’re already facing a similar crisis in game development as a whole, where a marketplace as big as Valve is littered with AI slop games while promising indie titles are hit with AI clones before they even get released.

When you get an add-on you want to use in WoW: Forever, installing it is easy. The installation process depends on how you want to approach it:

You can open the app and select World of Warcraft. Find the “WoW Forever” tab via the dropdown or by adding it from its list or scanning your computer. From there, you can see add-ons you can use. Select anything you like and click “Install.”

Find the .toc file of your add-on. Copy, cut, or move it to your local installation directory. It should be something like World of Warcraft/_forever_/Interface/AddOns.

From there, just open WoW: Forever, go to your options menu, and click “Add-ons.” Your recently installed add-on should be there. Enjoy!

World of Warcraft: Forever launches on November 4, 2026.

#3770. Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has much worse input lag than PS5

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has noticeably worse input lag than on PS5, which could put Nintendo players at a disadvantage in multiplayer.

Digital Foundry's tech review measured multiplayer latency at 81ms when docked and an average of 100ms in portable mode, against 49ms on PS5. Testing used wireless controllers on both consoles (a Switch 2 Pro Controller and a DualSense), and portable results ranged from 83ms at best to 125ms at worst.

Digital Foundry said "responsiveness here simply isn't as good as on other consoles", and described the lag in portable mode as "actually deleterious to performance" (thanks, IGN).

Beyond the lag, Digital Foundry is fairly positive about the port. Multiplayer runs at 60fps most of the time, and if your TV supports VRR, you'll notice the drops less. The campaign is capped at 30fps and resolution is dynamic.

Docked with DLSS on, the game targets 900p, but Digital Foundry saw it drop to 450p in busier scenes, such as the Paris vehicle chase. In portable mode, the target is 720p, with drops to 360p.

It's been 13 years since a Call of Duty game last appeared on Nintendo hardware, with Ghosts on Wii U in 2013. The series' return is the result of a 10-year deal Microsoft offered Nintendo while it sought regulatory approval for its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

#3769. Last Night’s VisionQuest Reveal Has A Whole Lot Of Marvel History Tied Up In It

VisionQuest has been pulling from a lot of the Marvel Cinematic Universeâs history, especially as it gets into the origins of artificial intelligence in the movies and delves into Visionâs relationship with his family. But last nightâs penultimate episode brought a character into the fold that some folks might not realize has some pretty significant history in the comic books as he was the first Human Torch, long before Johnny Storm took on the name in the Fantastic Four comics. Itâs time for a quick Marvel history lesson.

In the show, Paul Bettany plays J.I.M., also known as the Synthetic Man, and believe it or not, this guy is technically the first Marvel superhero, dating back to the first comic released under the brand in 1939. The character made his first appearance in the MCU in a brief cameo in Captain America: The First Avenger way back in 2011, but VisionQuest was the first time he had a proper speaking role. In the MCU, the Synthetic Man is the first of all synthetic life, and has become a cautionary tale for modern-day synthezoids like Vision because of the way he erupted into flame upon experiencing human-like emotion. He was created by Phineas Horton, who sought to rebuild his deceased son as an android, though his fixation on doing so lost him his family and fortune.Â

Their story has some more tragic consequences we wonât get into here, but the important bit here is that the Synthetic Man is the basis of all synthetic life in the MCU, and thatâs why Vision has traces of him in his code, and why they share the same face. Vision notes that J.I.M. âwears [his] face,â to which the Synthetic Man responds, âNo, you wear mine.âÂ

Though itâs not an exact adaptation of the comics, Vision and the Synthetic Man have a connection in the original story, as Vision was originally created from a copy of the androidâs body. However, because Visionâs creation differs in the MCU, with him being created from a robot body using the Mind Stone, this feels like Marvel bringing that connection back in a new way.

VisionQuest makes a point to never refer to him by his original superhero alias, which was, as many Marvel fans might not realize, the Human Torch. Most people know that as the superhero alias of Johnny Storm, one of the members of the Fantastic Four, an association strengthened by time and frequent appearances throughout modern Marvel media, leaving the android who held that mantle decades prior largely forgotten. VisionQuest hones in on the Synthetic Manâs inability to control his flames, but in the comics, he gains control of this power and uses it for good as a hero working alongside the likes of Namor and Captain America.Â

It remains to be seen if the Synthetic Man will play any major role in the MCU moving forward, but thatâs something we can speculate on further after next weekâs series finale premieres on November 10.

#3767. At Dead of Night sequel The Great Hugo is coming "(very) soon"

Baggy Cat Games, the team behind viral FMV horror game At Dead Of Night, has confirmed that a sequel is "coming (very) soon".

At Dead Of Night 2: The Great Hugo picks up where the original game left off and reunites us with Maya as she heads off to investigate a large Tudor manor house.

At Dead Of Night became famous quickly during the pandemic thanks to streamers and content creators like Markiplier, 8-BitRyan, John Wolfe, and DomPlays, who introduced us to Jimmy Hall, a creepy hotel landlord hellbent on recruiting an audience for his late-night comedy show and psychopathic comedy alter ego, Hugo Punch.

The new game, subtitled The Great Hugo, picks up half a decade later.

"Five years later, Maya is still haunted by her experiences in Sea View Hotel," the blurb teases. "Desperate for answers she remembers the ghost box she used in the hotel, left there when she escaped.

"After searching on [auction] sites and in antique shops, she finds a similar looking device, but can’t get it to work. She contacts an old friend and counsellor, Quinn, who had helped her understand her supernatural experiences in the hotel. Quinn recognises the device and knows where they were made - by an inventor who used to live in a large Tudor manor house not far from Sea View - but warns her against trying to get it working. However, Maya ignores his advice and goes on her own investigation."

Quite how long "(very) soon" is, we don't yet know, but we'll keep you posted.

It's been a good few months for Remedy Entertainment. In its latest financial results, the Finnish game developer announced that its third quarter revenue had more than tripled to €39.6 million ($44.3 million) from the €12.2 million ($13.7 million) it made during the same quarter last year.

That spike in income is all thanks to preorders and launch sales of Control Resonant—of which only the first seven days of sales were counted in Remedy's third quarter figures. On October 15, Resonant sold its millionth copy, making it the fastest-selling game in Remedy history.

"This is our first self-published game of this scale, built on our own Control IP," said Remedy CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon, who was appointed to the position earlier this year. "Praised by players and critics alike, it marks a defining milestone for the company."

Gaudechon also noted that "close to 50%" of Resonant players were Control newcomers, indicating the sequel had achieved "a key goal" of expanding the audience for Remedy's brand of stylish interdimensional sicko content. Its mission for the immediate future, the CEO said, is to continue delivering Resonant to more interested players—2.4 million of whom still have yet to turn their wishlists into purchases, according to Remedy data.

"Our priority now is to get Control Resonant into the hands of more players. Excellent player reviews, penetration in all our target markets and a substantial outstanding wishlist base give a solid foundation for the game's longer-term sales potential, supported by both organic visibility as well as our targeted marketing activities," Gaudechon said. "As with the launch, we will invest with discipline, prioritizing actions with a clear return."

While Remedy's operating profit margin was still thin for the quarter—1.5% of revenue, or €0.6 million—Resonant's strong launch performance is a welcome change of pace from where the studio was at the end of last year. In November 2025, it had posted an operating loss of €16.4 million thanks to the flop of FBC Firebreak. From the sounds of it, Remedy's aiming to continue that momentum with whatever work it has planned next.

"Alongside the launch of Control Resonant, our other projects are proceeding in the pipeline," Gaudechon said. "Sales over the remainder of the year will ultimately define our financial year 2026. Control Resonant gives us a solid foundation for growth."

#3765. Phantom Blade Zero is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, selling over 4 million copies in three days

Phantom Blade Zero studio S-Game has announced that its debut title has sold more than 4m copies in its first 72 hours on sale. The game's official X account broke the news alongside a celebratory message, though without providing a per-platform breakdown of copies sold.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support!" the developer wrote on X.

Phantom Blade Zero is available on Steam and PlayStation 5, but the 4m figure also includes sales made on the China-exclusive Tencent WeGame PC launcher. Prior to launch, Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott estimated Phantom Blade Zero to have sold over 1m copies before it had even released.

It was always clear the third-person character action game was going to be a hit, we just had to wait for actual figures to be released.

Phantom Blade Zero attracted over 431,000 concurrent players on Steam at launch, a figure that kept risking and rising into the weekend, ultimately settling at a massive 833,921 peak concurrent (via SteamDB). Just in case it wasn't already clear, this is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, beating the likes of Forza Horizon 6 and far outpacing all other major releases such as Onimusha: Way of the Sword, The Blood of Dawnwalker, and Ace Combat 8.

Despite the very strong opening weekend's numbers, Phantom Blade Zero has not been able to match or exceed the performance of Black Myth: Wukong, 2024's also-Chinese developed triple-A action game, just yet. The breakout hit, estimated to have sold 30m copies since, is one of Steam's largest debuts ever, peaking at 2,415,714 concurrent players at launch.

In Eurogamer's Phantom Blade Zero review, Emma Kent spoke highly of much of the game, but was critical of its underwhelming narrative and lack of consistency, writing: "This game is exceptional in so many areas - the animations, the beautiful environments - and when the combat works, the sense of flow is incredible. Then you walk into a boss battle and feel all that power fade, like you're waiting your turn to get hits in with a wooden sword."

#3764. Lore-Obsessed Fans Think The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel Is Connected To Skyrim

BethesdaSentinelSkyrimThe Elder ScrollsThe Elder Scrolls 6

Bethesda confirmed the title of the next Elder Scrolls game as Sentinel via a short non-gameplay teaser that, to many viewers, revealed the title and nothing else. But for lore-loving fans of the long-running RPG series, this small teaser has seemingly offered up some tantalizing hints about what to expect from the game and how it might connect to Skyrim and an ancient, mysterious order of magic users.

On Tuesday, Bethesda shared a small teaser for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. It was the first new teaser for the game since it was first announced back at E3 2018. The teaser features a quote from an in-universe character and also shows an Elder Scroll buried in sand being revealed by the winds. There’s some spiral imagery, too. And all of this is being analyzed by fans as they look to past Elder Scrolls games, like Skyrim, for possible answers.

First, let’s start with the quote. As pointed out by Reddit user HowdyHangman77, there’s actually quite a bit to pull from this snippet of text. For starters, the quote is dated 4E 206. This is just five years after the events of Skyrim. And considering Skyrimâthe province, that isâshares a large border with Hammerfell, it’s very likely that the events of Bethesda’s previous Elder Scrolls RPG, such as the return of dragons to Tamriel and the civil war between the Empire and the Stormcloaks, will be referenced or even directly seen in TES6.

Another interesting aspect of this quote is that it seems to reference alternate timelines or time travel, both concepts that have been established in Elder Scrolls lore. With previous reports that Sentinel will be about the origin of the Elder Scrolls themselves, perhaps some time travel shenanigans will be involved to let us see so far into the past.

Meanwhile, Reddit user Yiunko91 connected some of the circular rune patterns seen in the teaser with the Eye of Magnus, a very powerful magic item that first appeared in TESV: Skyrim. The Eye’s true purpose, origins, and power are never really explained in that game. And by the end of the Mage’s Guild questline, a mysterious, ancient group of magic users known as the Psijic Order shows up to take the Eye of Magnus away for safekeeping. These folks, according to past games and lore, love studying the ancient past and “Elder Ways.” Many fans have theorized that they’re interested in the Elder Scrolls, and hey, what do you know, there are lore connections between Magnus and the Scrolls. Oh, and in Skyrim it’s hinted that the Psijic Order might have time-traveled a unicorn to the future to save it from extinction. Hmmm…

Some are suggesting that the story of TES6 will be about a group trying to go back in time, possibly using the Eye of Magnus, to either stop the Scrolls from being created or to take them for themselves to use in some large-scale war.

Of course, we still don’t know how all these pieces connect. And it should be noted that this is all just speculation and theorycrafting by fans. So until Bethesda shares more, we’ll just have to wait. And that wait might be a while, as The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is reportedly still two years or more away from launch. Plenty of time to come up with even more theories.

Marty O’Donnell’s bid for Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District ended in disappointment—for Marty—as he’s one of many Republican candidates who got swept away by a massive blue wave that kept Democratic incumbent Susie Lee’s seat after a 20-percent margin of victory.

He served as Bungie’s main composer for over two decades, responsible for Destiny‘s soundtrack and, more importantly, Halo’s hauntingly beautiful main theme. Unfortunately, this really is a prime candidate for separating the art from the artist.

The first possibility is that Marty had received a glowing endorsement from Donald Trump shortly before the election.

It is my Great Honor to endorse America First Patriot, Marty O'Donnell, who is running to represent the incredible people of Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District. Marty is running against Susie Lee, a true Radical Left Extremist who does not represent the Values of Southern…

Unfortunately for O’Donnell, he was gunning for Nevada, a district that was greatly impacted by Trump’s unwavering stance on tariffs, so maybe that’s not the guy you want to seem very well connected to at that point. Still, there are other equally important reasons to point out, like the fact that O’Donnell is reportedly not someone you want close, or even “looming” around, especially if you’re a woman.

When talking about a particularly infamous event at a Bungie Halloween party, Marty said, “Yes, the women got really creeped out but I made sure to never touch anyone, just loom.”

After her tremendous victory, Susie Lee likely destroyed any horcruxes Marty likely still had lying around by tagging him in a tweet showing a viral video where a bunch of school kids perform a surprisingly beautiful rendition of the Halo theme inside a bathroom. The video fades to black with the message “the fight is finished.”

Enjoy your retirement @MartyTheElder pic.twitter.com/vH8KwKWrdl

I usually prefer when winners celebrate with grace and avoid teabagging their enemies, but Susie and so many others have been through so much crap because of “MartyTheElder” that I just cannot condemn anyone for double-tapping the guy.

As for Marty himself, well, he’d previously stated that he never really wanted to be a politician in the first place, so, if we’re to take his words for it, then everyone’s all the better for this result. Yes, even the people who cannot stop talking about how you shouldn’t be mixing politics with video games.

There might be hope for Arkane after all: A new report says multiple companies have made offers for it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new report from Bloomberg says Dishonored developer Arkane might not be as doomed as it appeared last month, as multiple companies have made offers to acquire the studio.

Citing "people familiar with the negotiations," the Bloomberg report says Ubisoft is among Arkane's suitors, as are at least two other unnamed gaming companies. Xbox has also considered selling the studio to its own management, effectively making it independent, although whether that option is still on the table isn't clear.

Despite producing an enviable slate of acclaimed immersive sims over the years (until it was compelled by senior leadership to do otherwise), Arkane fell victim to the Xbox "reset" in July that saw thousands of employees laid off (with more still awaiting their fates) and four studios cast adrift. Arkane avoided being the fifth, reportedly thanks to France's "Florange Law" that compelled Xbox to search for a buyer before pulling the plug.

The deadline for that search was November 13, after which Arkane would be shuttered—but a few weeks ahead of that date, Microsoft extended it by a month, to "explore options, including finding a partner to support the studio through the development work still ahead," a reference to the Marvel's Blade game Arkane currently has in development. That extension suggested there was at least some hope that Arkane might find a new home, instead of being closed.

Going from Xbox to Ubisoft could be viewed as a "frying pan to fire" move, given Ubisoft's own ongoing financial struggles, layoffs, and closures. But Arkane's immersive sim expertise could be a good fit for some of Ubisoft's biggest properties, including Assassin's Creed, Far Cry, and—yes, I'm just going to say it—Splinter Cell, which would be magnificent in the style of Dishonored. Arkane and Ubisoft both being French companies can't hurt, either.

I've reached out to Xbox and Ubisoft for comment on the report, and will update if I receive a reply.

#3761. Anker’s New Soundcore Space 2 Headphones Are Already 18% Off

Anker released the noise-cancelling Soundcore Space One headphones a few years ago, and while they were a more budget-friendly alternative to premium models from Bose and Sony, their performance and fit still fell short in several areas. The brand’s updated Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a major upgrade across the board: They’re comfier, have better ANC, and are currently 18% off at $106.49 (originally $129.99), a rare price cut for a still-new release from a popular brand.

Battery life is one of the Soundcore Space 2’s most attractive features: They last up to 50 hours with ANC on and 70 hours with ANC off, and a five-minute charge gives you up to four extra hours. The noise cancellation is strong for the price, blocking out lower-frequency sounds well. Comfort is also a major upgrade from its sparser predecessor, with roomier, more plush memory foam earcups and a padded headband. They’re also travel-friendly, as the earcups rotate and fold.

The Soundcore app allows you to customize EQ and sound presets, giving you added flexibility if you don’t like the default tuning. Instead of touch-sensitive panels, these headphones use conventional buttons, which help prevent accidental commands while adjusting the earcups and are easy to operate. Along with supporting Bluetooth 6.1, they also have a wired-cable option, which isn’t always the case with modern wireless headphones. That said, they don’t support USB-C audio.

If you want over-ear noise-canceling headphones that perform well but don’t have $200 to shell out for a more expensive model, the Anker Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a comfortable, effective, and long-lasting alternative that hover around $100 at the current discounted price.

Mainline Final Fantasy entries have taken a bit of a backseat in lieu of the FF7 remake trilogy, but that should be changing soon.

The trilogy’s producer Yoshinori Kitase teased the franchise’s future in a new interview, but I also wouldn’t hold my breath for Final Fantasy 17 launching any time soon after FF7 Revelation drops this April.

“I think that mainly we are more likely to invest in new titles and new games, but at the same time, for example, this time with the [FF7] remake, there was me and other creators who worked on the original game, which we had really strong feelings towards,” Kitase said when asked about new IP and remakes in the interview with IGN. “And we really wanted to create something new related to the old game to allow new users to play and to know the appeal of this game as much as the old users who play the old game. So there might be different cases like this one where the company is willing to invest in remaking old projects and other kinds of games like it happened this time.”

That’s…not really a definitive answer either way regarding remakes vs. new entries vs. new IP at Square, which is notoriously busy with multiple RPG releases year in and out across its numerous dev teams. For example, this year alone, the company has released Final Fantasy Resonance, The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales, Bravely Default Flying Fairy HD Remaster, and a few others.

Kitase’s words are iffy no matter how you look at it, but mainline FF entries have generally slowed down quite a bit. FF16 launched in 2023, but FF15 released way back in 2016. Meanwhile, FF7 trilogy games have come out in 2020, 2024, and next year again in 2027.

I’m generally a very big fan of the remake trilogy, and FF7 Revelation is one of my most anticipated titles of 2027, but I have a hard time imagining the company going on to remake another game… although I would not be against it, for several classic titles (6, 8, 9, or 10, please). Additionally, this year, FF Resonance has shown a true thirst and appreciation for classic turn-based games on top of the action-combat focus of recent titles, so I’ll be heavily tuned in to see what direction the series goes next.

Check out the full IGN interview for more from Kitase, including his thoughts on Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 being heavily inspired by Final Fantasy classics.

#3758. Soulframe to launch into free open beta this week, as Warframe devs go head-to-head with WoW: Forever

Soulframe's Preludes (its own version of a beta) is finally opening its doors to the whole world ahead of the Verse of the Veilands update. Starting this week, anyone who wants to can simply download the game and hop in, no invite required.

The date this happens is an interesting one: 6th November. That's two days after the release of World of Warcraft: Forever and the same week as Old School RuneScape's Hardcore worlds, so it's suddenly become a pretty packed month for MMO enthusiasts.

This comes after three years of closed testing for the fantasy action MMORPG, which players have been able to gradually see firsthand through sporadic invites. With Soulframe suffering delays since its first reveal, brief invite events have already occurred over this period. Even locked away, the game has received multiple substantial updates over the years, including new quests, Pacts (classes), factions and so on.

As for what newcomers to Soulframe can look forward to when Soulframe opens its doors, the Verse of the Veillands update is bringing a total overhaul of the map progression system this month. After the completion of an early quest, players are introduced to a corrupted landscape, the Veillands, which they must purify.

As you do so, new resources will be obtainable and side activities like fishing will be unlocked. You'll also be able to train up a small wolf pet into a full-on mount in the process. Previously, players were just thrust into the open world to explore and figure things out as they go, so this should provide something of an introduction to the game's open map. It won't be totally finished when released mind you, with updates to the Veillands system coming in the future.

On top of that, there's a new Pact called the Ode Shrike coming with the update. It's a tricksy trapper with spikes, balloon snares, bombs and chains to disrupt enemies as you whittle them down.

Could this be enough to win people over to Digital Extreme's newest project? Time will tell - but in the meantime its long-lasting sci-fi MMO Warframe is taking players to the Tau system in a major next step in the game's narrative this December. It comes with a detective noir inspired main quest, playable warframe, and even an in-universe Poker equivalent.

Mamdani and others have called out Google's decision to disable search functionality for schools who opt out of its AI tools.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Saying that it believes "schools should have control over AI in their classrooms," Google announced today that it will turn off access to its AI tools for K-12 student accounts. But there's a catch: Along with those AI tools, it will also disable Google search functionality.

In a blog post entitled "Designing responsible AI for learning," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, extolled the virtues of AI tools in "productive struggle," which he described as "enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up."

"That's the philosophy behind Guided Learning," Philips wrote. "In Gemini, Guided Learning acts as an interactive study tool that coaches students through the process of problem solving through open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns. Our research shows that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students, and we're now bringing Guided Learning to more products." Those products include Google Search and Google Classroom.

"After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search," Phillips continued. "Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on."

It sounds like Google Search on student accounts can be re-enabled separately, but that also ushers AI back into the equation: Google said in the update that it is "building Guided Learning capabilities into Search for student accounts to help them work through problems without skipping straight to answers." In other words, there is no search functionality on these accounts without AI intrusion.

Speaking to the New York Times, Phillips said "search and AI are deeply integrated," and confirmed that schools can't have one without the other: Students at schools that have turned off Google's AI tools "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Fairplay, a non-profit that aims to protect children from "the exploitative and harmful business practices of marketers and Big Tech," was somewhat harsher in its assessment. "Google's attempt to strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire," Fairplay executive director Josh Golin said in a statement. "Schools should use this opportunity not only to turn off AI, but to teach students that 'Google' isn't a verb, but the name of a surveillance and advertising company whose presence in schools has nothing to do with learning and everything to do with developing lifetime brand loyalty.

Former FTC chair Lina Khan, who was right about Microsoft's acquisition of Activision Blizzard, also weighed in, accusing Google of "using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI."

"Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened," Khan wrote on X. "As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don't fall in line."

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, a longstanding critic of oligopolies and corporate greed, said that "Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."

Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools. No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.  Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.

As NBC noted, research on the impact of AI in education is still quite limited, and some studies purporting to show meaningful benefits have been found to be flawed. That makes the headlong rush into AI integration, championed by massive AI companies and pretty much no one else, so controversial and potentially dangerous. Trying to force AI into classrooms while the technology's impact on mental health is an increasingly serious concern is audacious, and promises of more rigorous safety standards tend to ring hollow anyway: In October, the attorneys general for eight US states accused competing product OpenAI of ignoring its own safety warnings in pursuit of profit.

Google's new policy on AI in schools comes just days after shares in Google parent company Alphabet took a hammering as the company's AI Mode cut deep into its search business and revenue. I've reached out to Google for more information about the new educational policy and will update if I receive a reply.

#3755. 10 Shows Like 'A Different World' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The original A Different World was a groundbreaking sitcom in its era, spending six seasons highlighting Black academic drive among a cast of characters so indelible that we're now checking in on them decades later. Spearheaded by Queen Sugar's Felicia Pride, the update has been a critical and ratings hit for Netflix, earning the rarest prize of all in streaming television: a quick second season renewal. While you're waiting for season two, here are some other smart coming-of-age shows that blend heart and humor with realistic drama.

An easy pairing with A Different World, this show follows Black-ish's Zoey Johnson (Yara Shahidi) as she leaves home to attend a (fictional) California liberal arts college (the last couple of post-graduation seasons shift the focus to her brother Andre, played by Marcus Scribner). The emphasis is on driven young people who are capable of making big mistakes on the path to adulthood. A true comedy-drama, Grown-ish feels real(-ish) in a way that few other college shows have managed. Stream Grown-ish on Hulu.

Adapted from and expanding upon the 2014 movie, this show takes us to a (fictional) Ivy League school for a comedy-drama that tackles campus life and politics from a rather different perspective than that of Rooster. Logan Browning leads the ensemble cast as Sam White, who kind of inadvertently starts the titular radio show following a racially charged incident on campus. Far from the racial screed that some bad-faith YouTubers seem to find it, it's never shy about confronting the complicated and occasionally silly contradictions of campus activism, with each episode approaching life at Winchester University from a different character's perspective. Stream Dear White People on Netflix.

Kimberly (Pauline Chalamet) is an endlessly naïve scholarship student; Bela (Amrit Kaur) is an aspiring comedy writer on the make for the hottest guys; Whitney (Alyah Chanelle Scott) is an overachieving athlete and senator’s daughter; and Leighton (Reneé Rapp) is a closeted sorority girl. They're all randomly assigned to room together as freshmen at the fictional Essex College in Vermont. Created by Mindy Kaling and Justin Noble, this comedy-drama isn't nearly as salacious as its title suggests. There's sex for sure, but mostly it's a funny, queer-friendly show that's a little less about one overarching romance than it is about growing up, and the value of female friendship. Stream The Sex Lives of College Girls on HBO Max.

Even though we're backing up a couple of years to follow teens in their high school years, this British import's setting is a decent match, finding its students living away from home and family for the first time in their lives. At the fictional prestigious boarding school St. Gilbert’s, five Black teens are newly attending on scholarships, but their integration into the existing cliques is less than smooth—especially given that they're there largely as a PR stunt. Boarders blends teen romance, coming-of-age drama, and a delightful willingness to take the piss when it comes to the whole "rich private school" thing. Stream Boarders on Tubi.

Another modern take on a beloved '80s/'90s sitcom, this one's a bit different, serving as a total reimagining with no narrative connection to the original. And while A Different World is a comedy with dramatic heft, this one's more of a straight drama. It’s jarring for fans of the beloved original to tune in to find a serious show with the same premise as the Will Smith original—one that often leans into heavy realism. Jabari Banks plays, er, Will Smith, a 16-year-old from West Philadelphia who moves in with his auntie and uncle in Bel-Air following a gun charge and a run-in with a Philly drug lord. Banks is charismatic and believable, bringing a ton of personality to a show that occasionally veers down dark alleys. Stream Bel-Air on Peacock.

Comedian Benito Skinner plays himself, kinda, in this buzzy comedy that sees a former high school jock facing his freshman year in college while desperately trying to convince himself and everyone else that he's as straight as they come (relatable, except for the jock part). Much of the appeal is in its deft blending of tones: It's both a frequently raunchy college comedy and a sweet coming-of-age story about accepting yourself without worrying about what everyone else thinks. The cast includes Adam DiMarco (The White Lotus) and Rish Shah (Ms. Marvel), and, though it's more a story of one young man's coming of age, there's a strong ensemble backing him up. Stream Overcompensating on Prime Video.

The heart of All American (for most of its run) is Spencer James (Daniel Ezra), based on real-life NFL linebacker Spencer Paysinger. A star player for his high school team in Crenshaw, he's recruited by the coach (Taye Diggs) of a team in Beverly Hills to come and play for them, forcing Spencer to navigate two very different worlds while trying to build a life and potential career. Stream All American on Netflix.

Following a family tragedy, the already awkward 15-year-old Devi Vishwakumar (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) has a pretty terrible freshman year of high school, and decides that she’s going to turn things around the following year, hoping that a nearly academic study of sex will get her the boyfriend(s) her raging hormones have begun to demand. It works, to a point—but getting a surprise yes to sex from her crush leads her to question what she’s really ready for. More about burgeoning sexuality than sex specifically, this Mindy Kaling-produced series is both honest and charming. Stream Never Have I Ever on Netflix.

For realism in a show about the college experience, you could do a lot worse than this docuseries following several students at Gallaudet University, a school for deaf and hard-of-hearing young adults. In one sense, it's a specific setting where perspectives on deafness vary wildly, even in Gallaudet's self-contained world (aside from being a show about academically driven and horny college students, this is also a great primer for hearing people about some of the issues). But even for all of that, the challenges in building a life and future away from home are pretty universally relatable. Stream Deaf U on Netflix.

There's a reason A Different World has returned in 2026, and a lot of that has to do with the fact that there was nothing else on TV quite like it back in the late '80s and early '90s. For all of its sitcom sensibilities, the show tried hard (especially after multi-hyphenate creator Debbie Allen arrived to rework things after its first season) to paint a realistic picture of college life and an HBCU. Of the few shows on TV with largely Black casts, almost none would go so far as to highlight achievement and excellence; A Different World managed to do so while building a cast of characters so memorable that we're more than willing to catch up with them nearly forty years later. Stream A Different World on Netflix.

#3754. "We're doing great," says id Software boss, despite losing "about half of our studio" amid devastating Xbox cuts

Iconic Doom and Quake developer id Software was among the most heavily impacted Microsoft-owned studios during Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating business "reset" earlier this year, with around 136 employees reportedly losing their jobs.

In the wake of those layoffs, id Software co-studio director Marty Stratton was recently asked about the current state of the developer, and how it has been affected by Sharma's cuts. "We're doing great," Stratton told journalists at a recent event (via IGN).

"Not to handwave the [layoffs] away… everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that," he continued. "But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department."

This is not the first time a senior id Software member has pushed back on the narrative the studio has been "nerfed into the ground and gutted". Hugo Martin, id's other co-studio head previously claimed the remaining team is "the size we were when we made Doom 2016, and id Tech is very much alive and well".

Sharma's Xbox reset will ultimately see 3,200 jobs cut across Microsoft's gaming division, with many of those still to come. Those impacted by the first wave of cuts in July, however, included developers working on the id Software's id Tech engine. This is the engine behind all of the studio's games, and is known to be among the most performant engines, consistently producing visually-impressive games that require modest specs to run.

Following the layoffs, many inside and outside the studio said the id Tech team had been gutted. Longtime id Software programmer Chris Hays, who notably wasn't among those let go, said at the time, "It is hard to make a game that is triple-A, that is like we've done before, with half the people. And by hard I mean impossible". Hays also claimed "entire departments" and "entire disciplines" are gone.

While Stratton hasn't addressed those comments directly, he revealed id Software is now "working more closely than ever" with MachineGames, the Swedish studio behind the modern Wolfenstein games, and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. "We've always had a very close partnership with [MachineGames], but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]," he explained.

"We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that. We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead."

Id Software's next project remains unclear. MachineGames, on the other hand, recently said it's not done with Wolfenstein, so it's possible a sequel to 2017's The New Colossus is in the works.

#3753. Country of Fortune release countdown: Exact date and time

Country of Fortune is coming soon to gamers worldwide, and less than 24 hours are left for it to go live. Developed by Nepos Games, Country of Fortune takes city-building to a new level. Instead of constructing your city, you’ll be developing an entire nation, and every decision you make will have a key impact on your legacy.

But first, let’s find out when the upcoming nation-builder goes live.

Country of Fortune goes live worldwide on Thursday, November 5. The release date was announced by the developers earlier, and I am not expecting any change this late. The following countdown will expire once the game goes live.

The countdown is based on the following times.

If there is any change to the schedule ahead of launch, I will duly update it on this guide.

In Country of Fortune, you build an entire medieval country with the use of your settlements. The game uses grids, grows, and knits into a living region filled with people, rivers, and resources.

As a lokator, your first task is to pick a suitable grid to place your first settlement. Then, guide all your villages to help them grow from a hamlet to a bustling city.

Since no two grids are the same, you’ll need to adjust accordingly. There will be plenty of resource deposits to exploit, but you’ll be challenged by the environment and terrain.

With a wide economy, you’ll need to manage plenty of different aspects. Develop settlements and help them specialize in producing goods that require resources from the nearby areas. You can also develop roads and vehicles to set up a booming trade.

With different levels of power and endless micromanagement (if you want), Country of Fortune has plenty of exciting features to offer. If you’re unsure about what to expect, there’s a free demo available on Steam for you to try out ahead of the game’s early access launch.

As wishlisted games miss their release dates, Valve creates a new checklist to help devs get it right the first time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new kind of Steam problem has emerged: Games keep missing their release dates because Valve can't keep up with approving them.

Several frustrated indie devs have publicly posted about the limbo status of their finished games in the past week—including the developers of Food Devils, Wheel Make It, and Cubic Earth—saying that their applications have gone unanswered after up to 20 days, despite Valve's listed review window of three to five business days.

In the case of Cubic Earth, developer structmira hasn't been able to contact Valve and has no choice but to wait. "Our game's trailer amassed more than 60,000 views on YouTube, and we had more than 6,000 wishlists," the developer told PC Gamer over email. "Now, our Steam Community page is rapidly filling with player complaints, and we've lost all momentum."

Valve commented on the backlog today in the form of a Steamworks update aimed at helping developers pass the preview process. In it, the company admitted that it's "running a little behind" with wait times that are up to double the usual.

"We aim to test every game build in a timely manner, typically within 3-5 days. However, we're running a little behind right now and taking up to 12 business days," Valve's FAQ reads. "Much of that delay is due to having to re-review games, which isn't great for you or for us."

The update itself is, primarily, a new series of checklists that places the onus on developers to submit better applications that "pass review quickly the first time." The most significant new requirement is to have "run your game through Steam for at least five minutes" to make sure it functions correctly, which you'd think wouldn't need to be said. The tone of Valve's request suggests that it's also surprised by the state of some of the games it's being asked to approve..

"Believe it or not, sometimes we review builds that have not ever been played through Steam," the update reads. "This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam."

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Other checks include confirming which of those "common redistributables" a game needs before submission, confirming cloud saves and achievements are in order, and adding a minimum of five screenshots to the store page that depict gameplay (another obvious, but apparently necessary standard).

Though Valve did not comment on why a logjam in its processes has developed only recently, despite the number of new Steam games rising rapidly every year, the elephant in the room is AI.

New language models capable of whipping up functioning games very quickly, and Valve's laissez-faire curation, has prompted an explosion of AI slop games on Steam in the past few months—most of which don't receive much visibility, unless you're unlucky enough to browse Steam Next Fest without the "personalized" mode on. A Valve developer recently acknowledged that there's a slop problem on Steam, but said that they don't want to "be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn't use."

If you look at today's update through that lens, perhaps Valve isn't so much speaking to experienced developers with these obvious-sounding guidelines, but vibe coders who lack basic game dev understanding. Also today, Itch.io announced that it deleted "a couple terabytes of AI slop" from its videogame storefront to combat the wave of low-quality games appearing online.

Whatever the cause of the holdup, Valve said more changes are coming to the build review process, but this is a "great starting point."

#3750. How to get Apex Protocol Gear set in The Division 2

The Apex Protocol Gear set is a new addition to The Division 2, and it’s tied directly to the Echoes of Central Park DLC. The DLC has added a new playable area, and you get new bosses to kill.

These bosses are directly involved in providing you with the equipment pieces, but the job is easier said than done.

For starters, you will need to have access to the Echoes of Central Park DLC. Without it, you will not have access to the new location, which is mandatory for farming this gear set. As of writing, there is no other possible way to get the Apex Protocol gear pieces aside from playing in Central Park.

Once you have access to the location, your next task is to finish the main story campaign. It’s a relatively easy one, and you can also finish it as a beginner. Veterans can bring their Prototype gear, but the bonus effects will be unavailable at this location.

When you finish the campaign, you will learn about the Guardians. They were all former SHD agents who got involved in nefarious activities. This completely metamorphosed them and turned them into the apex predators. To get your gear pieces, you will need to defeat all of them.

There are five of them located all around the map, and you can see their locations on the image above. Head to the marked spot, and you will find the Lair of a Guardian. Once you reach a lair, you will have to deal enough damage to make the Guardian appear.

You will then have a set amount of time to kill the Guardian. As you deal damage, you will have the possibility of receiving the gear pieces as reward loot. The odds are not listed by Ubisoft, but they certainly go up at higher difficulties in my testing.

Hence, playing at Heroic will be the most rewarding thing if you do not mind the challenge and simply want to increase your luck of finding these pieces of gear.

#3749. Over a decade later, Bloodborne remains so popular it reportedly sold a quarter of a million copies this year alone

Bloodborne, FromSoftware's singular Lovecraftian action-RPG, has reportedly sold more than 251,000 copies this year alone.

That's according to Alinea Analytics head of market analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed the figure in a post on X, noting this brings Bloodborne's total sales up to an estimated 10.4m copies, generating $317m (around £236m) in revenue. Elliot also claimed more than half a million people played Bloodborne in October through PlayStation Plus.

Additionally, 12 percent of those are said to have played Elden Ring during the month, while 6 percent played Dark Souls 3, and 5 percent played Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. There's a cohort of gamers who are always bouncing between different From[Software] games," Elliott pointed out. "Can't blame them, especially with this one."

Bloodborne is a PlayStation exclusive that sadly never left the PS4, despite consistent calls from fans for ports and remasters. While the game is playable on PS5 through backwards compatibility, Bloodborne barely benefits from the console's advanced hardware, only seeing smoother frame pacing. In other words, it's the same game with barely any perceptible upgrades.

Before Sony closed down Demon's Souls remake developer Bluepoint Games earlier this year, the studio reportedly pitched a Bloodborne remake, but original developer FromSoftware didn't want it to happen. When news of the pitch came to light, former Sony Interactive Entertainment Shuhei Yoshida said Bloodborne has a special place in director Hidetaka Miyazaki's heart and speculated the reason it hasn't had a remake is because Miyazaki would prefer to do it himself but doesn't have the time.

"Miyazaki-san really, really loved Bloodborne, what he created," Yoshida said at the time. "So I think he is interested but he's so successful and he's so busy, so he cannot do it himself, and he doesn't want anyone else to touch it."
