#3675. Arkane union says closing the studio "would probably be more expensive" for Xbox than simply finishing Marvel's Blade

"Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic."

Xbox would probably spend more money shutting down Arkane Lyon than it would trying to finish and release Marvel's Blade, according to a union representing workers from the beloved imsim studio.

In a statement posted to the STJV (Syndicat des travailleureuses du jeu vidéo) website, the French union claimed that development on Marvel's Blade is "going fine" and is shaping up to be on par with Arkane's widely acclaimed gameography. By choosing to part ways with and potentially close the famed studio, the union says Microsoft is "sabotaging the game it funded."

After Xbox's sweeping job cuts and divestments from several first-party studios, Arkane was recently given until December to find a new buyer and ensure its future. Ubisoft Entertainment (Assassin's Creed, Rainbow Six) is reportedly one of the companies interested in buying the studio behind Dishonored, Prey and the upcoming superhero adaptation, though nothing has been finalised yet.

The union also blamed many of the studio's problems on Microsoft - a hiring freeze that lasted more than a year supposedly inflated the game's budget and caused additional internal delays. "Microsoft now use those same delay and additional costs as a reason to close the studio," the statement said.

"Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," it continued. "The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft's short term financial goals[...] The decision to close Arkane is solely the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization. Arkane is profitable. Just not profitable for Microsoft."

The union's list of demands now asks for employees to be able to have a say in choosing a potential buyer, as well as protections against any layoffs that might happen in the next few years. Should acquisition talks fail, the union claimed that the resources in Microsoft's redundancy package are "outrageously low" - so it's also demanding a redundancy payment of €200,000 per employee and further support.

Arkane's not the only developer reeling from Xbox's cuts. Double Fine (Psychonauts), Compulsion Games (South of Midnight) and Undead Labs (State of Decay) all managed to buy their independence, but had to lay off some staff as a result. It's not looking good for Hellblade developer Ninja Theory, either.

Liberty Mutual has gone too far with its latest ad campaign, and people are taking to the streets to protest it. While the general public often rallies behind commercials featuring popular actors or funny mascots, dozens gathered outside the headquarters of the insurance company to protest the existence of "Liberty Biberty." I'm sad I missed this protest, but I'm totally down to show up for the next one.

Led by YouTuber DimesAreTasty, people recently gathered in Boston in front of the Liberty Mutual headquarters to protest Liberty Biberty. Looks like the heat is officially off Limu Emu and Doug, because consumers decided they have bigger fish to fry.

In the words of the protest organizer himself, Liberty Biberty is a "nasty little pest" that was created by Liberty Mutual to "make the world worse." While his original video was directed specifically at how the new creature is a disgrace to all corporate mascots, the protest itself seemed to consist of people who were annoyed by seeing ads for the company while they watched sports or streamed shows with a Prime subscription.

The protest was only one day and only attracted dozens of people, and legitimate outlets like ABC News and others came out to cover the event. Unfortunately, I think the negative attention will only give Liberty Mutual more incentive to use the character, and maybe this all builds to a wild Super Bowl halftime ad. We shall see!

Liberty Biberty originally started as a joke in an older Liberty Mutual commercial, which featured an actor trying to say "Liberty Mutual" and instead saying "Liberty Biberty" instead. That character went on to do more commercials, with a running gag that he couldn't correctly say Liberty Mutual.

32 A-List Celebrities Who Have Appeared In TV Commercials

This gag evolved into a creature, which Liberty Mutual officially rolled out in July. The yellow fur ball was a puppet created in collaboration with the Jim Henson Workshop, so yes, I think that makes it a muppet. It's unlikely it'll be remembered as one of the best Muppets, but possibly the first to have a protest against it.

There is a part of me that suspects that Liberty Biberty was made in part to be annoying. The more people are making videos and content online about how much they hate the Liberty Mutual mascot, the more the company gets its name out there. It's not like having an annoying mascot is going to do much to impact the company's legacy and how it sells insurance. Heck, this might be the most I've talked about insurance all year, so if that was the play by the marketing team, kudos to them for pulling it off.

The Liberty Biberty ads will continue as the 2026 TV schedule rolls on. I'll be interested to see if any future ads address the backlash to the mascot, or if they'll phase out the mascot entirely after this negative attention.

#3673. What I Love (and What I Don't) About the New Una Fitness Watch

I’ve reviewed every type of fitness watch and thought I had seen it all, but my first glimpse of an Una watch had my jaw on the floor: There is a USB-C port on the side of the watch. Not a set of pins for a magnetic charger, or a socket that requires a proprietary cable—just a hole you can stick a regular old USB-C cable into. This is what watches have been missing.

The Una watch started popping up on my feed about two years ago, and finally started shipping this summer. I’ve been wearing a review unit for a few weeks. The Una watch is advertised as repairable and upgradable, with open source software. There are little screws that I can see around the watch face, and on the back panel. The Una website sells a replacement battery for $40 and a replacement screen for $50. They also sell the tiny screwdriver that you’ll need to make repairs, but if you’re the kind of person who gets excited about a repairable watch, you may already have your own.

Overall, I like it. The Una watch has an MIP screen (an older tech that is a cult favorite) and an app that's simple but effective. Not everything lived up to my expectations in testing, but no features failed outright. This feels like a solid start to the concept of “one watch for life” and I’m excited to see how the hardware and software offerings evolve over time.

Most wearables these days try to do as many jobs as possible, whether they’re the right tool for those jobs or not. I am honestly fine with a running watch measuring time, distance, and heart rate while I run, and not trying to score my sleep or pretend it can tell how fast I’m aging.

The Una watch app shows my steps, activity, and floors climbed for the day, as well as my average and resting heart rates. When I go for a run, it tracks my pace, distance, and heart rate during the run and gives me a nice page of data afterward. It reliably uploads this data to Strava, and can make little bar graphs of how these numbers vary from day to day.

There is a “store” (everything is free, as far as I can tell) where you can download extra watch faces and features. One I’m trying out is a habit tracker called HabitLab: It asks you every evening whether you had alcohol, cigarettes, a late meal, and so on. Every morning, it asks how you’re feeling. And then, even though the watch doesn’t normally track your sleep, the app takes note of your overnight HRV and resting heart rate. Over time, it will correlate the answers to those questions with the sleep data, to hopefully give results that are similar to Whoop’s journal analysis. (I haven’t been using it long enough to judge how well it works, but stay tuned.)

HabitLab appears in one area of the watch as a standalone app; another, called Gym Sets, gives me a strength training activity type, which the watch did not otherwise have. I just select Gym Sets instead of “Run” or “Workout,” and the app tracks my heart rate while also giving me a set timer.

The store is small, and the apps are simple, without many of the features that you can find on the apps for Apple Watch or other more fully featured devices. But the Una watch has only been out for a few months, so it’s not surprising that users haven’t created a plethora of apps yet. The company’s software development kit, and even its circuit board designs, are free for people to download and develop from.

I was worried that the emphasis on repairability, and the affordable price, meant that the Una watch would be made with components that maybe aren’t fully up to date. Heart rate sensors have been getting better over the years, so Una’s will have to be pretty good if it wants to even sit in the middle of the pack. Garmin, Apple, and now Fitbit have raised the bar quite a bit.

I will say the GPS track was reasonably good; on trail runs and road runs, it accurately followed the path I actually took. (It doesn’t seem to do quite as well as a new Garmin, but it’s still perfectly usable and its distance totals added up to reasonably accurate numbers.)

Heart rate accuracy disappointed me, though. When I first got the watch, the heart rate tracking was abysmal. I sent a few emails to my contact at Una, and almost had to publish this review with very bad news about the watch’s accuracy, but then a firmware update for the Una watch popped up on my phone. I installed it, and then tried another test run or two, and the heart rate accuracy is much better. If you get the watch, make sure it’s updated to at least 1.6.0.

That said, the update brought the heart rate accuracy to a level where I’d say it’s adequate, but it’s not good (and definitely not great). Its graph follows the ups and downs of my heart rate as measured by a chest strap, but sometimes the Una will spike and show a reading that’s significantly higher than my heart is actually beating. In the graph below, note the spike to around 165 when the true value was 155, and then later in the workout the Una watch detects another spike around 160 when my heart rate was actually around 145 and decreasing. (I saw similar anomalies in multiple workouts.)

In my time with the Una watch, many things made me happy. I still love the USB-C charging, and it was a delight to just plug it in to the same nightstand cable I normally use with my phone, no need to go looking for an adapter or dongle.

I like the MIP screen, which was brilliant in the sunlight and had a serviceable backlight for use indoors or in the dark. The small number of workout profiles and the small number of glances and apps is just fine if you’re not asking for much from a watch, and I wasn’t. It’s minimalist, low-distraction, and there isn’t a single AI-based feature anywhere. A true breath of fresh air.

And at $199, you’re not paying extra for these privileges. The price is just a little more than the new Fitbit Edge ($179.99), but less than a Coros Pace 4 ($249) or a Garmin 70 (also $249). The Una watch doesn’t have as many features or activities as these watches, but perhaps those pluses I mentioned make up for it.

The Una watch would be a good pick for someone who is excited about developing apps, wants a repairable watch, always loses charging adapters, or appreciates a minimalist approach. But would I recommend it for the average person who just wants a basic fitness watch? I’m not so sure.

The flaky heart rate sensor disqualifies it for a wearer who wants a more accurate, modern watch. The MIP screen is going to look old and weird to people who have gotten used to brighter, clearer AMOLED screens. The lack of sleep tracking or other convenience metrics may be hard to take when plenty of watches have these features.

So I like this watch today, with reservations, and I have high hopes for the future. If Una lives up to its vision, it’s going to be great to see replaceable components become available—perhaps there will be an option for an AMOLED screen for those who want it, and maybe there’s room for heart rate accuracy improvement in future firmware updates.

But a lot depends on the company itself. “One watch for life” implies that the company stays around long enough to make more than one model. I’m also hopeful that the future offerings will match what people want, and that the watch and app will stay uncluttered and subscription-free. But surely there will be competing interests that the company has to balance as they grow (if they grow), so time will tell whether the reality lives up to the vision. That said, I am liking the vision a lot.

#3672. This 'Nothing' Fitness Smartwatch Is on Sale for $59

If you haven't heard of the upstart tech brand Nothing, it's a UK-based company that aims to make products like cellphones and headphones with innovative features and designs—but at a lower price point than tech giants like Apple and Samsung. Last summer, the company released its newest smartwatch, the CMF Watch 3 Pro, which incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT, and you can currently pick it up at a major discount.

Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $59 at Amazon. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been, according to price-tracking tools.

According to Nothing, the CMF Watch 3 Pro is designed for "everyday users and casual fitness explorers." It quickly earned a reputation as one of the best budget smartwatch/fitness trackers of 2025. If you have a Nothing phone, the most noteworthy feature is its direct ChatGPT integration: You can use voice prompts to ask the chatbot questions or set reminders, among other things. Another neat feature, regardless of whether you have a Nothing phone or not, is its ability to record voices and auto-transcribe conversations or notes with the Nothing X app, which is great for work meetings or class.

If you've used the CMF Watch 2 Pro, you'll already be familiar with the design, which hasn't changed much. It still has a round display with a rotating crown on the top right, though the display is a bit bigger—1.43 inches compared to the Watch 2 Pro's 1.32 inches. Nothing has also kept the auto brightness adjustment, which is determined by a built-in sensor, and dual-band GPS support with access to five satellite systems, providing greater accuracy when tracking your outdoor activities.

The real upgrades come mainly from the software: The Watch 3 Pro has over 130 sport modes, compared to 120 on the older model. There's also AI tracking with personalized workout recommendations in real time. The battery now lasts 13 days on a single charge, which is two days longer than before. It's certainly in the running for the best sub-$100 fitness watch you can buy right now.

It's still early days for Warner Bros' new DC universe headed James Gunn and Peter Safran, but we just got one exciting update on one of the upcoming DC movies on the way. Dynamic Duo will officially star Mason Thames as Dick Grayson/Robin. It's perfect casting, especially since the actor once told us himself how much the character means to him.

In a new interview with Collider, Safran confirmed Thames casting, which has been rumored for awhile. Here's what he said about the 19-year-old from How To Train Your Dragon and The Black Phone movies earning the role.

We always talk about wanting volunteers and not recruits to be part of the DCU, to be part of DC Studios, and Mason always wanted to be Dick Grayson. He just did. And he came in, and auditioned the shit out of it, and was awesome. He's a wonderful young actor, but boy, did he want this. He was just obsessed. When he came over to the DC offices, he came over with his dad at the time, and we’ve got tons of great archives and stuff in there, and wanted to take a picture of everything and with everything. He's a fan.

When Mason Thames stopped by San Diego Comic-Con's suite back in July, he gushed with us about his deep love for the character. As he shared with us at the time:

I'm a big comic book nerd... Spider-Man's always been No. 1, but I love Robin, specifically Dick Grayson's Robin. I've loved his comic books. I have about a million of them. It's just fun to see his journey from him being first Robin to becoming Nightwing, to becoming kind of the symbol of what Batman wishes Batman was. And, he's always kind of been the best of him.

This new role for Mason Thames is absolutely deserved because he truly knows his stuff. In between chatting with him, I could see how genuinely stoked he was to be at his first San Diego Comic Con. He was asking me about all the tips to best enjoy the experience, and was hyped to walk the floor and get the full SDCC experience. He really and truly is one of us. Here's the video:

A post shared by CinemaBlend (@cinemablend)

DC's Dynamic Duo movie is set to have Thames' Dick Grayson working together with another Robin iteration, Jason Todd. Grayson grew up in a family of circus performers, but had to watch his parents fall to their deaths while trying to be complete one trick (after the act was sabotaged). He becomes Batman's first sidekick. Jason Todd, on the other hand, is a character who grew up on the streets of Gotham to a petty thief and a drug addict for parents before being taken in by Batman.

When the movie was announced it on X in October 2024, Gunn revealed it'd be "a mix of animation, puppetry, and CGI," making it a rather unique take on the characters. While Thames is presumably just taking on the voice role for Robin in this movie, Gunn has previously said this in 2023, per IGN:

And what we're doing with the DCU is we are having animation tied directly into live-action television and movies and games all intertwined within the same universe. We're going to cast actors that are going to be able to play the characters in this as well as in other things.

While we should keep in mind these comments are on the older side, Mason Thames looks absolutely ready to play Robin as is in live-action. And, I hope Dynamic Duo is the start of a long journey of the actor playing the role across a variety of mediums.

It's also worth nothing the movie is also produced by Matt Reeves, who's been the filmmaker behind The Batman films with Robert Pattinson. I wonder if we could see a version of his Dick Grayson in his universe? Dynamic Duo is set to hit theaters on September 22, 2028 following the release of Man of Tomorrow and The Batman: Part II next year. Congrats to Mason Thames on manifesting a dream role of his!

Now she's into covering YA television and movies, and plenty of horror. Word webslinger. All her writing should be read in Sarah Connor’s Terminator 2 voice over.

#3669. These High-End Marshall Headphones Are Under $200 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Marshall’s Monitor III ANC headphones have the kind of design that makes you want to show them off. The textured earcups and gold logo lean fully into the amp-inspired look, and at $199.99 (down from $379.99 at launch), they’re finally priced in a way that feels competitive. It's their lowest price ever, according to price trackers.

These are over-ear Bluetooth headphones with active noise cancellation, and they’re clearly aimed at people cross-shopping Bose and Sony. The difference is that Marshall is selling a vibe along with the sound. The build feels sturdy, and small details like replaceable ear cushions and a swappable silicone headband strap suggest they’re made to last longer than most. They fold down neatly into a compact hard case (included), but they’re not water-resistant, so they’re better suited for travel and home listening than sweaty workouts.

Living with them day to day is mostly smooth. The small gold joystick handles volume and track controls in a way that feels intuitive after a few minutes. There’s a separate button to toggle noise cancellation and transparency, plus a customizable shortcut button you can set up in the Marshall app. The app itself is simple, with a five-band EQ and a few presets, though it’s not especially deep if you like fine-tuning every frequency. Bluetooth 5.3 keeps connections stable, but you’re limited to AAC and SBC codecs, so there’s no hi-res audio support. You also can’t charge and listen through a traditional 3.5mm cable at the same time, since the single USB-C port handles both charging and wired playback.

Battery life is where these headphones truly stand out. Up to 70 hours with ANC on is more than enough for long trips, and turning ANC off stretches that to an almost excessive 100 hours. As for sound, they deliver strong bass and crisp highs, with enough punch to make hip-hop and electronic tracks feel lively. Noise cancellation reduces plane engine rumble and city noise well, but it does not match leaders like Bose in blocking midrange chatter, notes this PCMag review.

#3668. Ken Paxton: The Best Photos From the Texas Republican Senate Candidate’s “Come and Take It Tour”

Down in Texas, there’s an extraordinary Senate race unfolding between a deeply flawed candidate and a very surprising Democrat. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton overcame long-tenured incumbent John Cornyn in the Republican primary thanks to President Donald Trump’s endorsement, despite a long history of scandal. That background and Trump’s remarkable unpopularity have helped put the state within reach for James Talarico, a Democratic state lawmaker and pastor who maintains a steady but narrow lead in the polling. So this week, Trump rode down to the Lone Star State in an attempt to rescue his chosen candidate.

Vanity Fair’s Washington correspondent Aidan McLaughlin went down there too, and followed Paxton on his “Come and Take It Tour,” which culminated with a Trump rally in Corpus Christi. Photographer Mark Peterson joined him to capture the scenes. Here are the very best images from their jaunt across a state that could well determine whether Democrats seize control of both houses of Congress on Tuesday.

Disney has always been known for its animated blockbusters, but Frozen (which is streaming with a Disney+ subscription) became a full-blown sensation upon its release in 2013. Its sequel Frozen II crushed at the box office, and two more sequels were quickly announced. Although the studios' Head of Animation recently revealed a big change coming to the next two installments of the franchisee

The first Frozen III footage debuted at D23 over the summer, so anticipation for the threequel is steadily building. While we'll have to wait another year until it arrives in November of 2027, Disney's Jared Bush spoke to Collider about how the studio is approaching the next two movies. He revealed that they're putting a full emphasis on the third movie, rather than trying to put out 3 and 4 in quick succession. In his words:

Looking at Frozen 3 and what a Frozen 4 could look like, I know early on it was, 'We're going to put them right together, and they're going to be out in the world. It's going to happen quick.' That's not what we're doing, for a lot of reasons.

Rather than trying to produce a third and fourth Frozen movie as a cash grab (although they're sure to rake in the bucks), it sounds like the powers that be at Disney are putting story first. This is sure to be a relief for fans who might be worried about the property's legacy being soiled by the next two installments.

Fans are excited for Anna and Kristoff's wedding in the threequel, and to reportedly see Olaf get a love interest. Although we shouldn't expect Frozen III to do a bunch of set up for the developing fourth movie. As Bush went on to say:

To me, an important one is we want to make sure that Frozen 3 is the best movie it can possibly be, so that when you get to the end of the movie, do you feel like you've watched a complete story? That it feels like something that feels fulfilling. That doesn't always mean that everything is buttoned up, but it does mean that you have to be building to something that feels worthy of the end of a franchise that's that important to people.

Honestly, I love this strategy. Rather than getting too big picture about the Frozen franchise as a whole, it sounds like the next two installments will tell independent, fully formed stories. So we shouldn't expect any MCU-esque credits scene that help to set up the fourth movie once Frozen III hits theaters next year.

Sometimes thinking too far ahead can frustrate moviegoers when it comes to franchise films. For instance, Halloween Kills got some backlash upon its release for keeping Jamie Lee Curtis' Laurie Strode in the background and set up her role in the threequel. Luckily the third Frozen movie won't be doing that, and will instead tell its own complete narrative.

All will be revealed when Frozen III hits theaters November 24th, 2027. Since its not on the 2026 movie release list, we'll have to practice patience until footage get its wide release.

Social media is paying tribute to many influencers who died in 2026.

While recording a private New Year’s Eve livestream, Sergio Jiménez died at age 37. Days later, content creator Athira Auni died on January 3 at age 21 after a motorcycle accident.

In February, Chinnu Papu died by suicide at age 24. In March, Dominika “Mina” Elischerova, David Alejandro Peláez Marín — known online as Alejo Little — Rachel Tussey and Wang Weiqian all died. The next month, influencer Zepa died at age 26, Carlos Filhar died at age 48 and Mara Flávia died at age 38 and hiking influencer Ali Leiniö died at age 49.

In May, TikTok sensation Patriotic Kenny died at age 84 following a battle with stage 4 lung cancer. Later that month, Mexican influencer Paola Marquez was found dead in her apartment of a possible suicide.

In June, Yu-Gi-Oh! content creator Alex Cimo died at age 32 following a lengthy battle with stage 4 colon cancer. Later that month, Scary Mommy founder Jill Smokler died after being diagnosed with glioblastoma and cooking influencer Joel Yukich died after a “medical event.” Soon after, Gaby Sanarrucia Chavarria was reportedly shot dead in her home.

Influencer Laura Viktoria Härtig died at age 30 on July 12 after being involved in a head-on bicycle collision while on her honeymoon. Later in the month, Brazilian influencer Ulissias Marcelli and her boyfriend Vinícius Souza de Carvalho were found dead in a suspected shooting. Influencer Michael Selwood was also found dead on July 19, and Adriana García reportedly died the same month after undergoing a cosmetic procedure.

On July 23, TikTok influencer Sara Gilson was allegedly killed by her husband, Shawn Duffey, in a murder-suicide plot after publicly accusing him of pedophilia. Later that month, TikTok creator Rebecca Luna died after a battle with young-onset Alzheimer’s and chose to end her life by medical aid in dying.

In August, influencer Sofia Murillo died after she was involved in a helicopter crash in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Later that month, influencer Michiel Vandeweert died at age 28.

In October, fitness influencer and OnlyFans content creator Liam Fitzgerald died at age 29 following a motorcycle accident. The next month, TikTok star Marcel Johnson died at age 32 after a battle with stage IV stomach cancer.

A criminal investigation remains ongoing as of publication.

Runggaldier wrote via an Instagram statement, “Dear friends, in regard to the serious road accident in which I was involved, I ask you to respect my moment of pain and my need for confidentiality. My thoughts go out to all the people involved and their families. I trust in your sensitivity and please understand that at this time I will not give any interviews or statements.” Italy’s Trento Prosecutor’s Office is investigating the matter.

The video game influencer’s mother, Mary-Frances Alonzo, announced via LinkedIn that her son died in June following a battle with colon cancer. “Today, I have a very personal post to share as many of my colleagues are familiar with our journey. I know that he touched the lives of many of you.”

Indian influencer Nagalakshmi and husband Subramani were found dead at ages 41 and 51, respectively, after a suspected murder-suicide. Local outlets The Hindu and Times of India reported that the couple’s 18-year-old son returned to their home in Nanganallur, India, where he found his mother stabbed to death and his father dead in another room. However, they are investigating a possible third person's involvement because the door to the home was found open when the son arrived, according to reports.

Ben Wood, an American food and beer influencer, died on March 9 after trying to rescue a couple who were struggling in the water after being swept out to sea in Algarrobo, a coastal city in Chile. He was 43. Local news outlet BioBioChile reported that Wood, his father Norman Ray Wood, 77, his partner Maria Jose Duarte Ureta, 47, all died at the scene. Nigerian socialite Elena Jessica died after she reportedly underwent her second BBL surgery, her sister Nelli shared via TikTok. “My sister went to Cynosure and never came back the same,” she wrote in an emotional post on March 7. “Now she’s gone. 😭😭All I want is answers. All I want is justice. They can’t silence this.” Cynosure Aesthetic Plastic Surgery shared a statement regarding Elena’s death via Instagram, noting that a “patient” — presumably referring to the influencer — had sought a “corrective procedure” at their facility after she previously underwent a surgery at another clinic. She was later referred to another clinic for further care.  “However, the patient was subsequently taken to a different facility, a decision made outside of our hospital three weeks ago,” the statement continued. “We do herby empathize with the family of the deceased and pray for the repose of her soul.” Cynosure said it had “recorded zero patient deaths” this year.

After Derleya Alves underwent a breast augmentation on February 20, she reportedly began experiencing intense abdominal pain. She went on to have multiple tests and two additional surgeries, where her intestines were repaired and one of her ovaries were removed. Alves died on February 28 at Marabá Municipal Hospital in the Brazilian city of Marabá. According to the Daily Mail, the Marabá Municipal Hospital medical team "identified a possible congenital intestinal abnormality that may have contributed to the severity of her condition." Despite no suspicion of medical malpractice, information on Alves’ condition before the operation and her cause of death is pending.

Bianca Dias died days after undergoing a cosmetic surgery procedure. The Brazilian content creator died on February 19, according to her loved ones. News broke on January 19 that Ivonne Enriquez Ramirez died after being involved in a car accident. She was 20. Mexican newspaper Milenio reported that Enriquez was traveling on January 9 around 8 a.m. local time from the celebration of the town’s 487th anniversary with the mayor of the southern Mexican town Santa María Huatulco, Julio César Cárdenas Ortega. Spanish newspaper 20 Minutos reported that the vehicle overturned and fell into a ravine that was about 164 feet deep. “With deeply broken hearts, we share the painful passing of my beloved little sister Sweet Ivonne Enriquez Ramirez,” Ramirez’s sister Michel wrote in a statement via Facebook on January 19. “As a family, this moment breaks our souls. It's an immense pain, difficult to describe and even harder to accept. Nothing prepares us for a loss like this.” The statement continued, “We want to wholeheartedly thank each person who lifted up a prayer, sent a message, a word of encouragement or accompanied us with love during this very difficult time. Every show of love, every thought and every prayer reached us and held us up when we had no strength anymore.” The message shared that Ramirez left an “indelible mark” on their lives and hearts, adding that her memory will “live on forever in us.” The statement concluded, “We deeply appreciate your understanding and ask for respect in this difficult and painful situation as we go through this grieving process as a family.”

Spanish newspaper 20 Minutos reported that the vehicle overturned and fell into a ravine that was about 164 feet deep.

“With deeply broken hearts, we share the painful passing of my beloved little sister Sweet Ivonne Enriquez Ramirez,” Ramirez’s sister Michel wrote in a statement via Facebook on January 19. “As a family, this moment breaks our souls. It's an immense pain, difficult to describe and even harder to accept. Nothing prepares us for a loss like this.”

The statement continued, “We want to wholeheartedly thank each person who lifted up a prayer, sent a message, a word of encouragement or accompanied us with love during this very difficult time. Every show of love, every thought and every prayer reached us and held us up when we had no strength anymore.”

The message shared that Ramirez left an “indelible mark” on their lives and hearts, adding that her memory will “live on forever in us.” The statement concluded, “We deeply appreciate your understanding and ask for respect in this difficult and painful situation as we go through this grieving process as a family.”

Credit: Courtesy of Isaac Efraín Valadez/Facebook

Isaac Efraín Valadez was found dead on January 10 inside his truck with gunshot wounds. He was 44. Local newspaper El Heraldo de México reported that authorities in Ensenada, Mexico, were notified of an armed attack and found Valadez — who was known online as “Chakin Valadez” — dead at the scene before 7 a.m. The outlet reported that at least seven shots were fired. The Baja California State Attorney General's Office has not made any arrests in connection with Valadez’s death, according to the outlet.

Esther Thomas died on January 9 after undergoing surgery. “Greetings … We the family of Esther Thomas [A.K.A Sunshine] with pain in our heart we regret to announce the sudden demise of our beloved sister and daughter Esther Thomas who suddenly passed away on the 9th of January 2026 after an unsuccessful surgery,” a statement shared via Thomas’ Instagram read. “She had [a] fibroid and was operated on so she couldn’t make it so we are trying to put things in place so we could put her to rest.”

Credit: Courtesy of Isabel Veloso/Instagram

Isabel Veloso died at Hospital Erasto Gaertner in Curitiba, Brazil, on January 10, Brazilian outlet Mix Vale reported. She was 19. Veloso had been battling Hodgkin’s lymphoma since her diagnosis in 2021.

Sergio Jiménez reportedly died during a private New Year’s Eve livestream at age 37. Streamer Simón Pérez alleged on a January 4 YouTube livestream that Jiménez consumed six grams of cocaine on the night of his death. Pérez also claimed to be in contact with Jiménez’s brother, who reported that he had consumed whiskey in the final livestream. Mossos d'Esquadra — the police force in Catalonia, Spain — launched an investigation into Jiménez’s death, the outlet reported, with authorities ordering an autopsy on his body. Mossos d'Esquadra released a video on social media on January 6 encouraging people not to participate in “viral challenges” that could “put your life or your physical integrity in danger.” “The consequences of these trends can range from intoxication to physical and psychological effects, and can also have a negative impact on their reputation, affecting job and academic opportunities due to the digital footprint left behind,” an officer said in the clip, translated by People. “It's important to be aware that some trends can have consequences if they involve acts of vandalism or aggression.”

Nurul Athira Auni Mohamad Hafizzan, who went by the name Athira Auni online, died on January 3 at age 21. Local outlets Sinar Daily, Sinar Harian and New Straits Times reported that Auni was driving in the right lane when another motorcycle crashed into her from behind after swerving to attempt to avoid her vehicle. She was pronounced dead at the scene. The other motorcyclist faced injuries on his hands, elbows and thighs and received medical care at Tengku Ampuan Afzan Hospital. Auni’s body was transported to Tengku Ampuan Afzan Hospital for a post-mortem examination, according to local outlets. The case is under investigation for potential reckless or dangerous driving leading to death.

Yulia Burtseva died at age 38 after undergoing cosmetic surgery at a private clinic in Moscow on January 4. She was pronounced dead after being rushed to the hospital following her condition getting worse, according to Russian news outlet MSK1. While citing the Moscow Investigative Committee, MSK1 reported that the Main Investigative Directorate of the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation for Moscow has opened a criminal case to investigate potential negligence charges. "Investigators from the Moscow Investigative Committee are working at the scene,” a translated statement by the Moscow Investigative Committee and obtained by MSK1 read. “Necessary official and medical records will be seized shortly. A number of forensic examinations, including a medical one, are being ordered.”

#3665. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

#3664. Is This the Last Dance for Spain’s Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez?

On September 23, Maricarmen Abascal, a partially disabled 87-year-old woman, was evicted from the apartment she rented in Madrid, where she had lived her entire life. Suffering from exhaustion caused by the long struggle to keep her home and then her subsequent eviction, she was admitted to a hospital. That same day, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York, an international forum where he has often promoted his foreign policy agenda, beginning with his first visit in 2018, when the politician who had been given the nickname Mr. Handsome met many of his counterparts around the globe. While Abascal would never return to her home (she died on October 7), and her eviction sparked widespread public outrage, Sánchez spoke of reforming international organizations, criticized the United States and Israel, and called for reining in the “tech oligarchs” at the helm of social media platforms and artificial intelligence companies: “The future of our sons and daughters must take precedence over the financial interests of these techno-oligarchs.”

No one in Spain paid attention to the speech: Abascal’s eviction sparked social unrest in a country that boasts of being the fastest-growing in Europe in terms of GDP, a fact on which the Banco de España and the International Monetary Fund agree. This has positioned the country as one of the leading economies in the eurozone, with unemployment having fallen to historic lows, according to official figures. In macroeconomic terms, the country has consistently appealed to international investors during Sánchez’s eight years in office, with foreign investment having grown 34% since 2018, according to calculations by the Ministry of Economy. It’s possible that the Spanish economy is experiencing its best period of growth since the country’s return to democracy in the mid-1970s. However, inflation, housing affordability, and low wages—the minimum wage has risen from 735 euros to 1,221 euros, but has failed to boost salaries broadly—are taking a toll on this economic boom.

And, among voters, there’s a sense of mismanagement during this legislative term. There was the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the North African coast that saw the sudden arrival of more than 72,000 migrants in late July. (Ceuta has just over 83,000 residents.) The crisis was not enough to get Sánchez to cut short his vacation. It revealed clashes between the ministers of defense and the interior, and it has taken nearly three months for the situation to be brought fully under control. Political scientist and university professor Lluís Orriols noted in El Periódico that the government had come out “badly” in its handling of crises such as the one in Ceuta and the eviction of Abascal—problems compounded by “legislative paralysis” (the government has managed to pass fewer than 40 laws in this legislative session, down from more than 100 in the previous one) and “corruption.” He asserted that only the strength of the economy had prevented “a government in shambles.”

After elections in 2023, Sánchez managed to secure another term, but without a clear left-wing majority, he had to rely on the support of several right or center-right nationalist parties without a legislative pact, which led to numerous parliamentary defeats. The coalition has failed to provide Spain with an effective government. The international landscape has not been particularly favorable either. Sánchez has gradually lost his key allies: That group of young, charismatic left-wing leaders who seemed to set the global agenda and had a special rapport with the Spanish leader have long since left power—the photos showing the admiration for Sánchez from Sanna Marin of Finland, Justin Trudeau of Canada, and Jacinda Ardern of New Zealand are now a thing of the past. His rapport with other European leaders such as Emmanuel Macron, a relationship marked by effusive camaraderie since way back in 2018, is of little use now that France is in turmoil and advocates for a return to austerity are gaining power in Europe. Even his relationship with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission and one of Sánchez’s main supporters in the European Union, despite their ideological differences, is now of little relevance.

To top it all off, the prime minister came under fire even at Harvard, where he went shortly after his speech at the General Assembly to discuss AI, only to face sharp questions about Spanish politics and corruption. Even his safe role as a statesman was being eroded by political reality. Upon returning from his trip, an attempt to pass legislation that would prevent future situations like Abascal’s (in 2025 alone, there were more than 25,000 evictions, according to data from the General Council of the Judiciary) ran into obstacles in Spain’s fragmented parliament, which rejected every measure, and the legislative session came to a close. Meanwhile, the streets of Madrid and other cities began to fill with tents as people camped out in protest in a country where housing prices are rising by more than 10% annually, well above inflation and more so than wages. Whether it’s a matter of buying (nearly three out of every four Spaniards live in an owner-occupied home) or renting, both the Ministry of Housing and the real estate portal Idealista (which typically lists nearly half a million homes) reported price increases ranging from 30%–40% nationwide, going up to 70% in high-demand areas, during the eight-year period of progressive government, exceeding even the real estate bubble that triggered a 2008 crisis coinciding with the global financial crisis. The country is only just beginning to recover from its impact.

The half-hearted measures approved in previous years to tackle the problem ran into resistance from Spain’s regional governments and city councils controlled by the opposition—the center-right Partido Popular (PP), which governs 13 of Spain’s 19 regions. “Exactly,” the mayor of Madrid, José Luis Martínez-Almeida, said on X in 2021, when opponents accused him of doing “nothing” to tackle the rental crisis in the capital, where the average rent already exceeds the minimum wage.

On October 5, following a tumultuous legislative session in a divided Congress (the more powerful of the two houses in Spain’s parliament), Sánchez announced a snap election. Two days later, Maricarmen Abascal died in the hospital.

If Sánchez loses this election—and even the most optimistic nongovernmental polls, just over a month before the election, give him only between a 5% and 10% chance of winning another term—one of the world’s last bastions of social democracy will disappear along with him. Perhaps the most significant one, both because of the influence Spain has gained within the EU in recent decades and because of the personal leadership Sánchez has exercised in global geopolitics, with the prime minister having spoken out on issues such as climate change; digital governance of AI; the war in Gaza; and, in recent days, European support for Ukraine and migration management. This last issue has even pitted him against another of Europe’s last remaining social democrats (who is also in a precarious coalition), Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen. “Sánchez is the last social democrat who defends a migration policy that is compatible with human rights,” explains political scientist Pablo Simón, a university professor and specialist in electoral systems and political parties, “and he is committed to feminism and environmentalism. Once he leaves office, Spain will be more in line with the majority of Europe and its governments.”

Policies that Sánchez has implemented domestically include granting ministerial status to the 2030 Agenda, elevating the energy transition and the fight against climate change to the level of vice presidency during his terms, and creating the first agencies in any EU country dedicated to AI governance. He has also boasted about these achievements in flawless English—still a novelty among Spanish prime ministers, who have not been particularly fond of languages—at numerous international events. All of this has taken place at a time when the established world order is collapsing, and he has emerged as one of the world leaders who most vocally opposes Donald Trump. When he denied Trump the use of Spanish bases to attack Iran, he directly accused the American president of using “the smoke of war to hide his failure and, in the process, line the pockets of a select few.”

But support for Gaza (not only does Spain recognize Palestine as a state, but Sánchez has also strongly denounced Israel’s actions and labeled them as genocide) and opposition to warmongering leaders like Trump do not win elections on their own. “The debates in Spain are quite similar to those across Europe and focus on the cost of living and immigration, which explain the discontent with governments in many countries,” Simón explains, painting a picture that affects social democrats like Sánchez, leaders further to his right like Macron, and even hard-liners like Giorgia Meloni. The problems of inflation, low wages, loss of purchasing power, and strains on the welfare state are taking their toll on nearly every government in Europe.

Sánchez is, in fact, something of an anomaly with his eight years of resistance—he even titled his book about his political life Manual de Resistencia (Manual of Resistance). Looking ahead to these elections, it appears, on paper, almost impossible for Sánchez to retain his leadership. But if anything has defined his political career, it’s his ability to survive at the last moment, aided by the sociological realities of Spain. Ignacio Urquizu, director of Metroscopia and an election expert, explained a few days ago on SER, Spain’s leading radio network, that it “is the most left-leaning country in Europe, surpassed only by Malta.” He also noted that, since the 1980s, “there has been a straight line” showing that 45% of Spanish society consistently identifies as left-wing or center-left.

Sánchez has always relied on that reality for his historic comebacks. He went from being forced to resign in 2016 as secretary-general of the PSOE (the Spanish socialist party), under pressure from the party apparatus, to regaining that position just two years later and becoming prime minister on the back of a no-confidence motion against corruption, the first of its kind to succeed in Spain. The then future prime minister denounced the corruption that caused “embarrassment, disbelief, and outrage.” He has since survived two elections with the odds stacked against him, without clear majorities, in a Spain that is no longer defined by parties but by blocs, where different forces compete for similar political spaces, leading to parliaments that the framers of Spain’s constitution never anticipated.

The most dramatic of these occurred in 2023, when the right was already uncorking the Champagne, and a single member of parliament tipped the balance in favor of the socialist coalition. It was a poisoned chalice, as Spain has seen: The fact that the PP leader did not become prime minister, due to his failure to reach agreements with several nationalist right parties, paved the way for an ineffective legislative session, with 11 parties and a minority government entangled in parliamentary gridlock and social measures often being blocked by the “no” votes of Sánchez’s supposed allies. This miracle of resilience, in any case, has somehow lasted until now. Even so, Narciso Michavila, president of the social-research firm GAD3, is not ready to declare victory for the right just yet, despite what the polls say: Sánchez, he stated recently, “still has appeal,” and Michavila thinks it is still possible that he will ultimately secure another term.

But there is no denying that in the last decade in Spain, electoral politics have changed. Some of his loyal supporters during the period between 2016 and 2018 are now in prison or awaiting trial for the very corruption that Sánchez denounced. Former minister José Luis Ábalos, once his greatest supporter and whom he even mentioned in the no-confidence-motion speech that eventually led to his becoming prime minister, has now been given a 24-year prison sentence for corruption. Santos Cerdán, the man tasked with reining in the Socialist Party, is awaiting his turn in the dock. The party leadership that came to tackle corruption has proven to be just as, if not more, vulnerable to the recurring cancer of Spanish politics as those they replaced. And although Sánchez boasted about how quickly these incidents were dealt with (there are ministers from the previous administration who are still under investigation for corruption), he has long been unable to boast of integrity as he once did, now that scandals have involved his close associates.

Meanwhile, alongside these proceedings, Sánchez, his party, and many of his allies are denouncing the “judicial persecution” that has extended to the prime minister’s family—his wife, Begoña Gómez, is awaiting trial on various corruption charges, which the prosecutor’s office has opposed on the grounds of insufficient evidence (she has denied the allegations); his brother, David Sánchez, is appealing a nine-year disqualification from holding public office imposed on him by a court in Badajoz for administrative misconduct, stemming from his holding a public position as a cultural manager that was allegedly created specifically for him (he has denied the allegations). Pedro Sánchez has claimed that his brother and wife are “innocent” and victims of a “harassment and bullying operation.”

The latest chapter in this series of trials and investigations surrounding Sánchez was particularly painful for his party and his base: Former Socialist Party president and prime minister of Spain from 2004 to 2011 José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero (who was very active in the last election campaign and served as a role model for Sánchez and his vision of progressivism) was indicted in spring 2026 over an alleged corruption scheme. Jewelry valued at more than a million euros, which Zapatero took months to clarify was supposedly a gift from the Saudi monarchy, was discovered during the searches and sealed his fate. (He has denied any wrongdoing.) The role model Sánchez had looked up to and who boasted of having led the least corrupt government in the history of Spain’s democracy suddenly became the first former prime minister in the country’s democratic history to testify as a defendant. The case is still in the preliminary investigation phase.

But at first, the PSOE came out in force, through press releases and statements from its leaders, to denounce the alleged act of lawfare with the phrase “Whoever can act, should act.” It was a direct quote from the former president of the Partido Popular, José María Aznar, when he attempted to rally opposition to Sánchez’s alliance with Catalan parties in 2023.

These tensions within his family and his party, and the blurring of the lines between the two that the opposition accuses him of, have also spilled over into his campaign. This has put his wife and the developments in her legal case in the spotlight. Sánchez declared he was “deeply in love with” Gómez when he threatened to resign in 2024, following the media harassment of her. “They’ve tried to break us in every way possible, and they’ve achieved exactly the opposite; today we’re more united and stronger than ever,” the prime minister told his wife. “Let them hear it loud and clear: I love you.” The prime minister and his wife’s campaign kisses date back to at least 2016, but this time the Socialist Party has taken up the cause: “We are the party of love,” declared Minister Óscar Puente, and the prime minister has even worn a T-shirt bearing the campaign slogan “La Fuerza del Amor” (“The Power of Love”).

Meanwhile, the far right is poised to become the country’s third-largest political force, now that measures to contain it have failed in Spain, as they have elsewhere in Europe. No measures have succeeded in curbing its rise—or, in cases like Italy, its success at claiming direct power. Spain has, however, long been a country that leans more to the left; it is perhaps the most socially left-leaning country in all of Europe.

“The truth is that the Iberian Peninsula as a whole leans a bit further to the left than its neighbors due to its historical legacy,” says Simón. “In fact, because of this history, socialist parties fare better in Spain and Portugal, and they also do well in the Scandinavian countries.” On the other hand, one need only look at France, where the once all-powerful Socialist Party is now politically irrelevant, to understand the situation in much of the rest of Europe, where centrist parties have lost their influence.

It was the mobilization of Spain’s historic left-leaning majority that saved the PSOE in 2023. This had repercussions in Europe: While other social democratic leaders were falling and the centrists or moderate right-wingers were losing momentum, Sánchez became the voice of a progressive Europe. Emmanuel Macron, who, with Sánchez, built a sort of Spanish-French axis within the European Union, now watches as France burns, six months before an election in which the far right is almost guaranteed to reach at least the runoff round. And all this is unfolding in the midst of what has been described as “Russiagate,” with “foreign interference in all democratic processes in the European Union, including disinformation.”

For Europe, the consequences of this electoral process have already become apparent: The Union had to decide on a far-reaching budget, which also includes the future of Ukraine—whose president has warned that the country needs an additional 70 billion euros that Europe does not currently have. This is especially true following the revelation by Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, that the EU has been left on its own in its contribution to Ukraine’s defense and rearmament: “Since January of last year, the United States has not contributed a single cent to Ukraine’s defense. We, Europe, are doing it.” But the elections in Spain are the start of a chain of electoral contests—France and Italy will follow—that push the possibility of an agreement further out of reach. European negotiations often drag on for years, and any electoral upheaval can derail those already underway. One of Sánchez’s most loyal ministers, Luis Planas, for example, will not appear on any electoral lists so he can devote all his time in office to these negotiations: “Between now and the end of the year, the future of the common agricultural policy and the fisheries policy is at stake,” which in Spain accounts for nearly 9% of GDP through both direct and indirect contributions.

The elections will be held on November 29 amid a tense atmosphere: The right is resorting to personal attacks and AI-generated deepfakes against Sánchez, his wife, and his cabinet. Left-wing forces have not found a figurehead like Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party and are polling at less than 10%—a situation that would leave the PSOE without strong coalition partners even if it performs well. Sánchez’s international standing and the strength of the macroeconomy will likely have little weight in an election where the focus is on basic issues including the cost of living and specifically housing. But whatever the outcome, it will likely be the first in a series of elections that may lay bare the crisis facing liberal democracies in Europe. Now without the protection of the United States, it faces two existential crises. There’s an internal crisis, marked by the rise of the far right and its contempt for human rights, and an external crisis, with the Russian threat becoming clearer by the day and commercial and technological pressure from the United States and China, which has counted Sánchez among its most important advocates in its dealings with Europe.

This story was originally published by Vanity Fair España. It was translated by John Newton.

#3663. South Of Midnight Director Says He Would Not Have Funded The Game

Xbox funded and published 2025's South of Midnight, a highly acclaimed action-adventure game set in the American Deep South. The game's creative director, David Sears, said he believes South of Midnight is a "generational" game that he hopes people discover and play for a long time and one that he thought would help elevate the "prestige" of Xbox.

At the same time, Sears said he wasn't sure Microsoft's spending spree under the previous leaders Phil Spencer and Sarah Bond--which is how Sears' studio Compulsion got the funding to make South of Midnight--was going to work out long term.

"I literally told people, I was like, 'Yeah, wow, this could be terrible.' Because somebody is going to say, someday, 'The money tap ... we're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream," he told Ben Hanson on MinnMax.

Microsoft spent billions and billions of dollars to buy studios and franchises to help get Xbox Game Pass off the ground. The bet did not work out, and now Spencer and Bond are out. The new Xbox CEO is Asha Sharma, and one of her first moves was to cut costs dramatically with layoffs, studio divestures--including Compulsion--and game cancellations. Sharma also talked about how Game Pass needs to evolve into something that's "more enticing to a broader range of customers.”

Asked directly if he had been in control of the Xbox funding at the time, would Sears have stopped writing checks for games like South of Midnight? "Yeah, probably," he answered (via Kotaku).

"I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously. Because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah. Because I’m not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable," Sears said.

A lot of people said Microsoft's spending on Xbox Game Pass was unsustainable and ultimately going to lead to pain and turmoil. Raphael Colantonio, the co-founder of Arkane, said Game Pass is unsustainable and "increasingly damaging" to the industry. Game Pass has been propped up by Microsoft's "infinite money," Colantonio said.

Raccoon Logic studio head Alex Hutchinson spoke out about Game Pass devaluing games earlier this year after his game Revenge of the Savage Planet was a day-one title on Xbox Game Pass. Conversely, Rebellion touted the launch of Atomfall on Game Pass as a huge success for the company.

With Microsoft's big bets not panning out in the way the company envisioned, the Xbox business struggled, and the ensuing Xbox "reset" has been painful for the people, teams, and fans of Xbox. Sears said hindsight is 20/20, but he always had a feeling that things just weren't right and that the bottom could fall out one day in terms of Xbox's spending spree.

"Of course it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. It’s easy to dissect it now. But at the time ... I would talk to other directors and [they’d] be like, 'How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like ... 'For now,'" he said. "And there’s always a night when Rome burns. I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Sears went on to say the Microsoft of today is "much more humane" than the company was in the '90s and 2000s, something he said is "remarkable and commendable."

Sears said it's a good thing that Microsoft is allowing studios it wants to let go of get spun out instead of shutting them down outright. Compulsion, for its part, was among the studios that got spun out, and is now operating independently and seeking new projects and funding sources.

South of Midnight originally launched for Xbox and PC in April 2025, later coming to PS5 and Switch 2 in March 2026. Now that Compulsion is independent, buying the game supports the studio directly, and not Xbox.

Throughout all of the downturns at Xbox, Microsoft continues to make gigantic sums of money, in part because Xbox represents just a tiny sliver of the company's overall business. For the latest quarter, Microsoft made $92.3 billion in revenue (up 19%) and a profit of $36.6 billion (up 32%). Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has praised Sharma for gutting the Xbox business so heavily.

Hailey Bieber had a big October. She knows it too, posting a full thread to Instagram at the end of the month simply captioned “Thanks October” and featuring her in an angel Halloween costume. In Mr and Mrs Smith, Jolie’s “Jane Smith” is out on assignment and shows up in a full bondage outfit complete with tall boots, a spandex dress and mesh elbow gloves with confusing purpose. A post shared by amber asaly (@amberasaly)

#3661. Buying GTA 6 Could Save You $5,000, Or At Least This Guy Thinks So

Self-made millionaire Mark Tilbury has shared some advice for how buying GTA 6 can actually save you $5,000. Just don't take this too seriously.

Here's how he arrived at that number: If the game costs $100 (for the Ultimate Edition) and it takes 80 hours to complete, that works out to $1.25/hour of "fun." After adding on side missions and simply exploring GTA 6's map, investing in the game seems like an even better deal at just 50 cents of fun per hour.

If you play for four hours every evening, that's 50 nights of entertainment. Tilbury said people should compare this to a night out where they could easily spend $100 in a night.

"That's why buying GTA 6 actually saves you $5,000," Tilbury says.

Even if it's not a full $100, Tilbury is spot-on that going out to do most things today costs a pretty penny. So staying in to play GTA 6 may indeed "save" you some money you might have spent elsewhere. You may also play a lot of GTA 6 and continue to go out and spend money on other things.

His math also might be conservative, as people are no doubt going to play GTA 6 for far more than 50 days, especially when GTA Online 2.0 releases in 2027, as expected.

Clearly, though, Tilbury is being cheeky here and created the clip for virality and for people to send to their friends and partners to justify how much they are going to play GTA 6.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and a PC edition is expected to be released in 2027.

#3660. TikTok Star Marcel Johnson Dead at 32 After Stomach Cancer Battle

TikTok star Marcel Johnson has died after a battle with stage IV stomach cancer. He was 32.

“November 2 2026 @ 445pm. I lost a whole entire half of me,” Johnson’s wife, Taylor, wrote via Instagram on Tuesday, November 3. “He fought so hard for so long. He was so tired & exhausted & in so much pain. Yesterday the only words Marcel said all day were to me & Dedric and it was ‘I’m ready to go’ and that was in the morning. He still fought to hang on all day so we just got a bit more time.”

Alongside the message, Taylor shared a series of photos of the couple through the years, some of which included their five children.

“I truly don’t even have words right now,” she continued. “I feel like this can’t be real life. How can this be real f***ing life. I thought I was going to wake up and he was still going to be here beside me. I love him with my whole entire being and life will absolutely never ever be the same. @celnoshell.”

While a GoFundMe was previously created to support Johnson financially during his cancer battle, the fundraiser is now being used to help his family in the wake of his death. More than $370,000 has been raised at the time of publication.

“Hi everyone, as you probably know now, Marcel has passed away after a long and tough battle of Stage 4 Stomach Cancer,” a message read on the GoFundMe page. “He beat the odds the doctor gave him but ultimately he was at peace and ready to not be in pain.”

The statement continued, “We are now raising money for Taylor and their beautiful five boys during this rough time. Anything is appreciated! ❤️.”

Johnson was diagnosed with stage four stomach cancer in August 2025 and chronicled his journey via social media for more than 200,000 Instagram followers. He underwent 25 rounds of chemotherapy before ceasing treatment in September.

“Update, no more chemo, I’m too weak for treatment,” he wrote via Instagram at the time. “Update 2. Hopice [sic] has been calling everyday to ask I’m I’m ready bedtime [sic] have no more options. Update 3 if I can make it to Oct 15 and strong enough to travel I’ll go to my appointment at city of hope in Cali. But I gotta make it there first 💪🏽🙏🏽.”

The next month, Johnson and Taylor uploaded an Instagram video of themselves flying on a private plane to the City of Hope Medical Center in California. Days later, Johnson shared via Instagram he was returning home and “got some answers” that he “needed.”
